members.text: Warm-lane recovery gotcha: a task's full implementation can already be committed on its task/NNNN branch when the architect is (re-)invoked, because `acquire_lane` re-seeds the worktree from base and wipes the gitignored `.task/plan.json`. In that case the architect should reconstruct a plan matching the existing TDD commits (git log main..HEAD shows the test/impl pairs) rather than call report_task_already_done — that tool requires the work be on main, but here it is on the unlanded branch. Reconstructing plan.json regenerates the artifact the orchestrator state machine needs so the task can proceed to verify/land.

CONSOLIDATED (merged 11 near-duplicate entries total: 5 in the 2026-07-05 partial merge + 6 residual near-duplicates folded 2026-07-05 per task 5022): Warm-lane task resume / requeue-rebase loses `.task/plan.json` (gitignored, filesystem-only per CLAUDE.md — never survives a lane re-seed) while the branch's committed TDD step commits (`test(NNNN): step-K RED` / `feat(NNNN): step-K GREEN`, sometimes prereq tags like `pre-1`) survive intact on task/NNNN. Trigger signatures: task metadata `reblock_guard` reading like "warm-lane acquire fault for branch 'NNNN' (seed/worktree...)"; an architect re-invoked and finding branch commits but no plan.json; branch annotated "RESUME CONTEXT: this is a re-queue"; or a requeued task surfaced with a DIFFERENT task's plan.json attached (a prior lane-occupant's, or an adjacent sibling task's — verify plan.json.task_id actually matches the dispatched task before trusting it). Correct action: RECONSTRUCT a faithful plan.json mirroring the committed step structure — `git log --oneline main..HEAD` (or against the branch's merge-base) plus per-commit `--stat`/diff to map each commit to its step by touched files — then call mark_step_done per commit and let the executor re-verify the already-GREEN steps rather than redoing them. Do NOT call report_task_already_done: that path requires the commit be reachable from main, and task-branch WIP is not. Verify premises against the live worktree diff (`git diff <base_commit>..HEAD`) before reconstructing; don't trust old commit-message "green" claims or a plan's analysis narrative blindly — re-run the actual tests/clippy first.

Task-specific gotchas to check every time (kept separate as they carry unique detail):
- A "chore: save WIP before rebase" commit can contain a REAL step's full implementation, not just noise — always `git show --stat`/`git show` each WIP-labeled commit before dismissing it (task 4168, memory a5e8b6b4-10f5-4d43-8b7e-f0cadd54e7bb).
- TDD commits can be directly S1..SN-labelled enabling 1:1 mapping, with a WIP commit occupying the slot of the step whose label was stripped during rebase (task 4870, memory b28158fb-2bdf-408b-979c-03f71cc11520).
- Interleaved WIP-save commits and step-pairs that share one commit SHA both occur — use the last commit in such a sequence as the step's recorded commit (task 4954, memory 17b3b5aa-39b0-4750-b6b5-d552081ac563; also task 3965, memory 1ccfce69-dec1-4a6d-ad1a-81e0440107f9).
- Trailing WIP commits beyond the last clean step commit can be folded into one clean commit via `git reset --soft <last-clean-step-sha>` + recommit — verify `git rev-parse HEAD^{tree}` is unchanged before/after to prove no content was lost (memory 57af0b70-d339-49ea-a203-6732b588bf47).
- Extra WIP commits after the last named step can contain legitimate additional task-scoped hardening already absorbed into an existing step's description — these don't need a new plan step, just re-verification that they still pass (task 4942, memory a7e90820-babc-4d09-9a27-05a81222ed24).
- A prior LANE OCCUPANT's stale plan.json can be shown for the current task (task 4019 shown task 3932's plan) — verify plan.json.task_id matches the dispatched task (memory e44cd1f5-0696-4fa2-899b-842fc61368e6).
- A SIBLING task's plan.json can be shown instead (task 4855 shown task 4854's plan) — verify actual branch state (git log/rev-list) before trusting the shown plan (memory 7b0d9518-e1ee-4f3e-b86c-f62a399b709a).
- After an INFRA-failure requeue mid-implementation, a rebase during "save WIP" commits can rewrite SHAs, so a reconstructed plan's recorded SHAs for already-"done" steps can point at the wrong (later WIP/amend) commit — don't trust recorded SHAs at face value; cross-check `git log --format='%H %s' main..HEAD` against the plan's file list (task 4906, memory fe1e9c21-0b65-49a5-88b5-bed9225037fa).

Architect plans must declare in `files` only paths the task will WRITE, not paths it merely reads or calls into. The pre-merge phantom-done gate flags any declared file untouched by branch commits and forces a narrowing pass. Task 5334 (δ cluster formation) declared crates/reify-eval/src/structural_query.rs defensively, but its expansion helpers (build_trait_registry, enumerate_descendants, expand_structural_query, apply_trait_filters, apply_cost_aggregation) are already `pub(crate)` on main and callable from resolve_order.rs with no visibility widening — so the file was consumed read-only and had to be dropped from the plan.

Architect resume gotcha (warm lanes): when re-invoked on a task/NNNN branch, the prior run's .task/plan.json can be gone (.task/ is gitignored, wiped on warm-lane re-seed) while its committed TDD work PERSISTS on the branch. Always `git log --oneline main..HEAD` first — if commits already implement part of the task, plan ONLY the remaining gap (don't re-plan already-green RED tests), but still list the full task footprint in create_plan files[] so locks/phantom-done see all branch-vs-base diffs. Seen on task 5031 (gui-state-sync L2): diff.rs + L1 lint + bridge.ts were committed; only engineStore.ts frontend transport remained.

Architect resume gotcha: when re-invoked on a task branch that already has a complete TDD commit sequence but is missing .task/plan.json, and those commits are NOT yet on main (unlanded on the task branch), reconstruct a faithful plan mirroring the committed steps and confirm_plan() — do NOT call report_task_already_done (it requires the commit be reachable from main and would fail that validation for unlanded task-branch work). Observed on task 4971 (verify.sh nextest-probe fix): 4 commits a70958eb80..0eb2201908 present, plan.json absent.

An architect can be re-invoked on a task branch that ALREADY carries complete committed work: `.task/plan.json` is untracked, so a warm-lane re-seed (tracked-files-only + `git clean -xfd`, e.g. when the branch is rebased onto a new main tip) wipes it while the commits survive. Diagnose with `git log --oneline main..HEAD`. The correct response is to reconstruct a plan whose steps map to the existing commits — NOT `report_task_already_done`, which requires the commit to be on main (verify with `git ls-tree main -- <path>`; a branch-only commit does not qualify).

claim: When resumed on a task branch, `.task/plan.json` may be missing while committed work survives; inspect the branch and reconstruct a faithful plan instead of reporting the task done.

members.text: Host sweeps this Claude session's harness-tracked background tasks roughly hourly (observed 2026-07-25: the L2 watcher + a run_in_background sweep were both KILLED ~twice/hour). The killed-task NOTIFICATION is itself a re-establish trigger — relaunch on it. But for a helper LOOP that doesn't need to notify the agent (e.g. a merge-worktree reclaim sweep), run it setsid-detached (`setsid nohup script > log 2>&1 </dev/null &`) so it survives sweeps; give it a self-terminate guard (grep the watcher-<project> lease file for your own slug each cycle → exit when released) plus a MAX_CYCLES backstop, and have it write a status file per cycle the agent can poll. The L2 WATCHER itself must stay a normal run_in_background task (it needs the harness fire-notification), so it stays sweep-vulnerable and is relaunched on each kill. Also: killed /spawn wrappers do NOT kill the spawned session (it detaches into its own terminal) — verify via ps + read result.md.

OPERATIONAL GOTCHA (killing background builds from an interactive Claude Bash tool): broad process-killing patterns can match the harness's OWN command subshell and truncate the command (observed as exit 144 = 128+SIGTERM, or "Killed" mid-output). Specifically `kill -TERM -<PGID>` where the PGID is shared by the tool's subshell, and `pkill -f 'cargo build --workspace'` (matches the literal pattern string inside your own running command line). Safer: kill explicit PIDs, or pkill on a path unique to the target (e.g. the lane's absolute target dir) that cannot appear in your own command. The actual build processes still died correctly each time; only the reporting command self-terminated. The persisted log files survive, so just re-read them in a follow-up command.

`pkill -f <pattern>` and `pgrep -f <pattern>` match against the FULL command line, which INCLUDES the running shell's own command containing that pattern string — so `pkill -f phase0-run.sh` or `pkill -f load-sampler.sh` self-matches and kills your own bash (observed twice jun9 2026, exit 144). Always kill background helper scripts by PID (capture from pgrep output, then `kill <pid>`), not by `pkill -f <name>` when <name> appears in your command. Also note: multi-statement Bash tool commands occasionally get mangled by the harness's eval-wrapper collapsing newlines between statements (e.g. `tail -8` invalid, echoes concatenated); prefer one logical command per call or `&&` chains, and `tail -n N` not `tail -N`.

Shell gotcha (cost ~40 min wasted wall-clock 2026-07-25): checking background-build liveness with `pgrep -f "cargo build -p reify-cli"` SELF-MATCHES — the checking shell's own command line contains the pattern, so the check reports "still running" forever (the build had finished in 2m35s). Same family as the probe-exit-pipe gotcha. Robust alternatives: grep the build log for `Finished`/`error`, test the target binary's mtime, or pgrep with a pattern the checker doesn't carry (e.g. `pgrep -x cargo` scoped by cwd, or `pgrep -f 'carg[o] build'` bracket trick). Also applies inside `until pgrep ...` watcher loops — the loop matches itself and never exits.

claim: Process checks and kills using broad command-line patterns can match the shell running them; use explicit PIDs or independent evidence such as logs and artifacts.

members.text: reify-eval test-harness consolidation (task #5278, PRD merge-gate-compile-cost.md C1/leaf EVAL-1, "1/3" of 3) verified pattern for sibling leaves 2/3 & 3/3: move standalone crates/reify-eval/tests/<file>.rs into tests/harness_<sub>/<file>.rs and declare each in tests/harness_<sub>.rs via `#[path="harness_<sub>/<file>.rs"] mod <file>;` (explicit #[path] REQUIRED — a bare `mod` at an integration-test crate root resolves to the sibling tests/<file>.rs, not the subdir). This prefixes every test's nextest name with `<file>::`, so `test(/^<file>::/)` selects exactly that former binary's tests; consolidation is selection-neutral because NO .config/nextest.toml or tests/infra filterset references reify-eval test files by name (only the 7 override binaries use binary()). Three gotchas confirmed: (1) source-relative include_str!/include_bytes! need exactly one extra `../` when moved one dir deeper (e.g. fixtures/ -> ../fixtures/, ../../../examples/ -> ../../../../examples/); concat!(env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR"),...) loads are move-safe and must NOT be touched. A successful `cargo nextest list -p reify-eval` already PROVES include-path correctness since include_str! resolves at compile time. (2) Files installing a process-wide #[global_allocator] (common::alloc_counter::CountingAllocator) must stay STANDALONE + grandfathered in tests/infra/harness-layout-baseline.manifest — two in one binary is a "multiple global allocators" compile error, one shared corrupts sibling alloc-count deltas. (3) Ratchet: remove each moved file's `crates/reify-eval/tests/<file>.rs` row from the baseline manifest IN THE SAME DIFF. Cost gotcha: alternating `cargo nextest list --workspace` and `-p reify-eval` triggers full ~7min recompiles (feature unification differs) — pick ONE invocation form and stick to it. Layout-only: BT-1 total #[test]-fn count must be unchanged (reify-eval was 4690).

Reify compiler: a sibling-let geometry reference lowers to `GeomRef::Sub(name)` ONLY on the Modify/Transform/Pattern argument path (the #4668 bare-Ident pre-check, crates/reify-compiler/src/geometry.rs:1377-1385). Boolean operands go through `resolve_boolean_arg` (crates/reify-compiler/src/geometry_boolean.rs:28-60), which has no bare-Ident pre-check and INLINES the operand's initializer as sub-ops referenced by `GeomRef::Step(n)`. Measured: for `param geometry = difference(body, holes)` the names "body"/"holes" appear nowhere in the compiled realization's operations (only `Sub("hole")`, from the Pattern arg, survives). So `RealizationDecl.operations` — and `reify_eval::deps::extract_realization_edges`, which shares the blind spot — is NOT a complete oracle for "which sibling realizations are consumed downstream". The complete name-level source is the value-cell layer: `TopologyTemplate.value_cells[*].default_expr` carries `ValueRef(ValueCellId{entity, member})` for every sibling reference. Caveat when using it: a `: Rigid` structure's auto-derived mass/centroid/moment_of_inertia lets also hold `ValueRef(geometry)`, so a consumption scan must count only Geometry-typed cells as consumers.</content>
</invoke>

STAGE 1 FLAG FOR STAGE 2 (run_id=48f39a36-30c6-45a4-a88d-5e5fb1e0cb9e): Mem0 entries 7489bac8-d7f7-4467-8161-8077e13cb1e1 (2026-07-26T04:11:52, observations_and_summaries) and c759c53b-9506-41d8-858f-fb882c7e297f (2026-07-26T04:39:28, observations_and_summaries) contradict on reify compiler sibling-geometry consumption semantics. 7489bac8 characterizes reify-eval's extract_realization_edges match arms (Boolean{left,right}, Modify|Transform|Pattern{target}, Sweep{profiles}, Isosurface{grid}) as "the authoritative enumeration of which CompiledGeometryOp variants carry consumption edges." c759c53b presents an empirical measurement (param geometry = difference(body, holes)) showing Boolean operands do NOT surface as GeomRef::Sub refs to sibling lets at all — reify-compiler's resolve_boolean_arg (geometry_boolean.rs:28-60) has no bare-Ident pre-check and inlines the operand's initializer as GeomRef::Step sub-ops instead, and explicitly states extract_realization_edges "is NOT a complete oracle for which sibling realizations are consumed downstream." Both entries carry substantial unique, non-overlapping technical detail (distinct file:line citations, the bare-name/dotted-name Sub-ref convention, the value-cell-layer fallback) — resolving which characterization is authoritative requires reify-compiler domain judgment, not a mechanical merge, so Stage 1 is not resolving this silently per the conservative safe-vs-irreversible consolidation rule. Recommend a Human curator gate task (matching this project's established pattern for Mem0 consolidation ambiguities, e.g. tasks 5552/5541/5537/5534) to adjudicate and consolidate these two entries.

Sibling-geometry consumption edges are already encoded in the compiler output: a `let` that references a sibling geometry `let` lowers to `GeomRef::Sub(bare_name)` inside `RealizationDecl.operations`. Bare names (0 dots) mean same-structure siblings; dotted names ("sub.member") mean cross-sub — a namespace split that is safe by construction since DSL identifiers never contain '.'. The authoritative enumeration of which `CompiledGeometryOp` variants carry consumption edges is the private `extract_realization_edges` in crates/reify-eval/src/deps.rs: Boolean{left,right}, Modify|Transform|Pattern{target}, Sweep{profiles}, Isosurface{grid}; GeomRef::Step(_) is intra-node and skipped; Primitive/Curve/Profile carry none. It is not re-exported through `pub mod deps`, so consumers outside reify-eval (e.g. gui/src-tauri) must mirror its match arms rather than call it — cite it in a comment so the two cannot drift.

claim: Before consolidating reify notes, verify behavior against the implementation and tests; apparent compiler-edge accounts conflict, so require domain judgment rather than silently choosing one.

members.text: Gotcha found planning task 8124 (T3 lane γ): once session hooks read T3CODE_THREAD_ID, a hook test run from inside a T3 thread leaks that var into `session_hooks.main` (it reads os.environ), so hand-launched test records would be claimed as display.kind t3 and get a sessions-by-t3-thread pointer. orchestrator/tests/_session_hook_fixtures.py::isolate_hook_env must scrub T3CODE_THREAD_ID alongside CLAUDE_SPAWN_*. Also: spawn_t3_lane.py::_is_hand_launched's `not is_t3_record` clause becomes wrong once hook-made hand records for T3 threads are t3; result_file None alone tells a hand record apart (a spawn record always has one).

Gotcha from task 8124 (T3 lane gamma) for orchestrator/tests/test_spawn_t3_lane.py: `launch` sweeps (mark_t3_sessions_exited) BEFORE it sends t3_thread_launch, and the fake t3_thread_list answers with no threads. A t3 hand record you create with the real session_hooks.run_session_start(..., {'T3CODE_THREAD_ID': THREAD_ID}) before calling launch is therefore swept as an orphan (ORPHAN_EXIT_CODE) and never folded. To test the race where the hook fires first, run the hook from inside a callable 't3_thread_launch' responder on FakeT3Server. The hook then runs after the sweep and before the record stamp, which is the real order of events.

Gotcha (task 8124): T3 thread ids are not always UUIDs. A UI-started thread's T3CODE_THREAD_ID is a bare UUID, but an MCP-started thread's is `mcp:<uuid>`, and a t3_thread_launch thread's is `mcp:launch:<64 hex>`. So any file-name or token check on a thread id must admit ':'. The Claude session-id token class (session_registry.py::_SESSION_ID_RE) rejects these ids, and reusing it blocked every lane thread from being indexed under sessions-by-t3-thread/. Use orchestrator/src/orchestrator/session_registry.py::is_t3_thread_pointer_name ([A-Za-z0-9:-]{1,128}), and build test fixtures with the real mcp:launch:<hex> shape rather than a UUID or a 'th-...' placeholder.

claim: T3 session hooks and indexing must account for real thread IDs and launch ordering, while tests isolate inherited environment and simulate hooks after the orphan sweep.

AMENDMENT-PASS PRECEDENT (task 4823, commit 16a902a476) — a rung-1-shaped case (the reviewer's own wording offers two alternatives) with a distinction the ladder does not yet name: the alternatives were NOT equally valid, and the decisive test was not "which one conflicts with a design decision" but "can the proposed check ever actually fire".

THE CASE. A reviewer flagged a genuine residual gap: `df_pytest_isolation.py::deploy_clock_change_report` attributes a moved deploy clock by parsing only the END-of-session snapshot, so a test falsification that a GENUINE redeploy later overwrites on the same clock inside one run reads as benign and the run goes green. The reviewer offered two remedies: (a) "at minimum, name this second gap in the same THE RESIDUAL GAP paragraph"; (b) "if you want coverage rather than documentation, the cheap version is to also parse the BEFORE entry's provenance and force 'falsified' when either snapshot carries this session's token, plus a test".

WHAT DECIDED IT. Trace the proposed check's INPUT against the producer's actual call order before accepting it. Here the fixture generates its per-session token, stamps it into the environment, and only THEN takes the `before` snapshot — so `before` is read before any test has run and can never carry this run's own token. The suggested branch is unreachable in production; it would have been exercised only by a synthetic unit-test input. Worse, it does not close the gap it was offered for: the falsified body is overwritten mid-run and is never in `before` at all. Shipping it would read as coverage while providing none — strictly worse than the documentation option, because the next reader would believe the gap was closed.

THE GENERALISABLE TEST, for any reviewer suggestion of the shape "also check X": (1) name the concrete producer of X and its call order; (2) enumerate the values X can actually hold at the check point; (3) ask whether the failure scenario the reviewer described puts the incriminating value into X. If (3) is no, the patch is decorative — take the documentation alternative and record in the docstring WHY the cheap patch does not work, so it is not re-proposed at the next review. Do not add an unreachable defensive branch merely because a reviewer named it: an always-false branch is not fail-closed, it is noise, and it converts an honestly-documented boundary into a false claim of coverage.

WHAT WAS SHIPPED INSTEAD: the gap named explicitly as "(2) AN OVERWRITTEN FALSIFICATION" alongside the pre-existing lost-token gap, with its narrowness quantified (needs both writes to one clock inside the same 26-41 min run against an 8h redeploy cadence), the refutation of the cheap patch stated inline, and the real fix named (continuous/intermediate observation — a per-test guard or a file watch — which is exactly the cost the fixture documents rejecting when it chose SESSION scope). The test class that pins the adjacent case now says it is CROSS-clock only and points at the gap, so its silence reads as a boundary rather than an omission.

GOTCHA when a code review asks for a test pinning a "documented but untested" internal branch: MUTATE THE CODE FIRST AND RUN THE SUITE, because your own amendment may have just made that branch unobservable — in which case the correct deliverable is a docstring correction, not a test.

MEASURED, task 5319 (dark-factory, commit c97322b727). A reviewer filed two findings on `dashboard/src/dashboard/http_pool.py`: (1) `reap_orphaned_connections` frees pool slots but never calls httpcore's `_assign_requests_to_connections`, so requests already parked in `wait_for_connection` are never dispatched and die on their pool timeout; (2) the function's two suppressed-failure paths — `suppress(Exception)` around `await connection.aclose()` in phase 2, and a deliberately SEPARATE phase-3 removal loop — are "precisely the branches a later simplification would collapse without any test going red", so pin them.

Fixing (1) added a phase 4 that runs `_assign_requests_to_connections()`. That silently invalidated half of (2). Mutation-tested each claim rather than assuming:
  - drop phase 3's `suppress(ValueError)` -> 1 test red. Good.
  - move `closed += 1` outside phase 2's suppression -> 1 test red. Good.
  - MERGE phases 2 and 3 into one loop (the exact "later simplification" the reviewer named) -> 29 passed, nothing red.
The merge is invisible because `AsyncHTTP11Connection.aclose` sets `_state = CLOSED` BEFORE awaiting the network stream's close, so a connection whose close raised is still `is_closed()`, and phase 4's `_assign_requests_to_connections` reclaims it through httpcore's own `is_closed()` branch. The new phase absorbed the old phase's only externally-visible effect.

WHAT WAS DONE, and why it is the right call: keep phase 3 (it states "a sweep unpools what it doomed" directly, instead of inheriting the guarantee from a private httpcore reclaim branch a shape guard cannot check and a future release may narrow), CORRECT the docstrings that claimed the two loops were separately observable, and do NOT write a test pinning the loop structure. A test that can only see the difference by reaching into `pool._connections` mid-sweep is the "tests reaching a module's internals is an interface-design smell" stance in CLAUDE.md, and it would ossify an implementation detail the public contract no longer distinguishes. The test that WAS written pins the observable contract instead: a close that raises is not counted as a clean reclaim, and the connection is unpooled anyway.

THE GENERAL RULE. A review finding of the form "branch X is untested and a refactor would collapse it silently" contains an empirical claim — that collapsing X is observable. It is cheap to check (one mutation, one suite run) and it goes stale the moment anything else in the same function changes. Check it in the same pass that changes the function. If the mutation survives, you have learned something the reviewer could not have known, and the honest output is a corrected comment plus a note in the commit message — not a test manufactured to make the finding true.

Amendment-pass precedent, task 4565 (commits 02e5ea8e45 + 79ade07433), extending the "reviewer suggestion vs. frozen plan" cluster (4188 narrow-apply, 4705 pick-the-review's-own-alternative, 2618 documentation-only-alternative, 2548 verify-the-escape-hatch, 4751 verify-the-premises). Adds the INVERSE of 4751 MODE 1.

4751 MODE 1 recorded a failed premise making a SKIP cheap to justify. The inverse also happens and resolves differently: a suggestion's premise can be measurably WRONG while its complaint still stands on other grounds — and then the move is to apply a CORRECTED version of the fix, not to skip on the failed premise.

MEASURED INSTANCE. A reviewer asked to delete two of three near-identical `TestThe*LoadedOnceNotReExecuted` classes, arguing the harvest copy's docstring imported an inapplicable hazard because "exactly one test module registers the harvest key". Grepping the key found TWO registrations (test_harvest_production_queries.py's own `_load_module()` and test_read_transform_selection.py:2988's `_load_script(HARVEST_PATH, ...)`), so the premise was false. But the core complaint survived independently: the copied hazard — `read_transform_selection::_load_script` serving `sys.modules[name]` by name only — genuinely cannot reach that key, since that bootstrap has exactly one caller and it passes 'bake_off_storage_shape'. So the docstring really did mislead about why the test exists. Resolution: take the review's own stated-minimum alternative (rewrite the rationale, keep the test — plan step-9 mandates one such test in each of three modules by name), and write the NARROWER TRUE rationale the measurement revealed rather than the one the review proposed. Commit message records both the correction and why the delete option was declined.

SECOND LESSON, on "this assertion doesn't actually discriminate" findings: prove it with the mutation, do not reason about it. The review claimed a queries-half test would still pass if its call site were mislabelled `kind='probes'`. Applying exactly that one-token mutation produced `1 failed, 3 passed`, failing only on the newly added `assert 'queries' in message` — which simultaneously confirmed the gap was real, confirmed the new assertion closes it, and confirmed it is a real discriminator rather than a wording pin. Backup the file to /tmp and restore from there; never `git stash` in a dark-factory checkout.

claim: Verify review claims against actual execution or mutation before adding tests or fixes, and preserve only independently justified, observable behavior.

members.text: CORRECTION + RECURRENCE for the drain-gate TimeoutExpired budget gotcha (amends memory d81a4f56-9f3a-4c0e-b5fe-a432c033ddc9, which says the fix was "Raised to 15s under task 3269" — the task attribution is wrong AND the fix has since been reverted and re-broke). Actual history for scripts/tests/test_restart_all_orchestrators.py::test_defer_withholds_restart_while_busy: commit e73e2da759 (2026-08-07, "give the drain-defer test enough budget to reach its own assertion") raised its subprocess timeout 3 -> 15, recording min 0.85s / mean 1.34s / max 3.00s time-to-defer-line at load ~100 on 32 cores. Commit 127549662c (2026-08-08, task 3798, "shrink the three 27.8h grace knobs to a derived 30s/80s") reverted it to 3 the NEXT DAY as collateral of an unrelated refactor: it replaced ORCH_RESTART_FORCE_FIRE_AFTER_SECS="99999" with wait_proof_grace_secs(spawn_timeout), needed some spawn_timeout to derive from, and took 3 from the adjacent test_unknown_grace_withholds_restart_while_absent (where 3 IS legitimate, because that test asserts only the monotone "no restart recorded"). Nothing in the repo could fail on the revert, so it survived 11 days until it failed a full scripts/tests/ run and cost task 4085's implementer an investigation (task 4218, escalations agent-followup-4085 / esc-4218-1). The mirror assertion in tests/scripts/test_orchestrator_watchdog.py::test_boundary4_defers_busy_unit_while_others_proceed independently needed the same fix (8s -> 20s). GENERAL LESSON, applicable beyond this file: for a load-flake fixed by widening a single timing literal, the widening is not the deliverable — the number has already been widened and un-widened here. Land it as (a) ONE shared constant both call sites import (df_pytest_isolation is the right home for the scripts/tests <-> tests/scripts pair, since those two roots cannot import each other's test modules but both import it), and (b) a BEHAVIOURAL guard that goes RED when the number shrinks — for a subprocess-latency flake, a PATH shim that sleeps before exec'ing the real interpreter reproduces spawn starvation deterministically (wall-clock sleep, not CPU-bound, so the guard is not itself load-sensitive).

Gotcha (stdlib subprocess wrappers), second confirmed site — see existing entry 033a3698-8b6a-4e00-a9a0-22886d4e369e (task 2980, scripts/reclaim_orphaned_worktrees.py `_run_git`) for the original: `subprocess.TimeoutExpired` and `subprocess.CalledProcessError` are `SubprocessError` subclasses, NOT `OSError` subclasses. A never-raise subprocess helper guarded only by `except OSError` still raises on timeout. Task 3642 found the identical gap in tests/scripts/test_know_live_installed_unit_parity.py's `_systemctl_user_show` — its docstring promised "Returns None — never raises" for a `systemctl --user show ... timeout=30` call, but a wedged systemd --user manager / stuck D-Bus produced an uncaught `subprocess.TimeoutExpired` instead of the documented skip. Confirms the pattern is not specific to retention-sweep scripts. Refined fix recommendation over the original entry: prefer `except (OSError, subprocess.SubprocessError)` (the common base) rather than enumerating `except (OSError, subprocess.TimeoutExpired)` alone — SubprocessError also covers CalledProcessError, which matters if a caller ever adds `check=True`. Do not widen further to a bare `except Exception`, which would also swallow genuine programming defects (e.g. a TypeError building argv) and convert them into a silent skip. This entry should be consolidated into 033a3698 by a recon-stage agent (I lack content_amend authorization as a task-implementer agent_id).

DeterministicRunner before_done subprocess hang (tasks 2087/2090): `_default_run_script`'s timeout branch (deterministic_runner.py) called `proc.kill()` on ONLY the direct bash child. Scripts like restart-fused-memory.sh --drain spawn grandchildren (systemctl restart, curl, journalctl, the restarted daemon) that inherit the merged stdout pipe's write-end, so `proc.communicate()` never sees EOF and the reap/cancel can hang past timeout_secs; also `proc.kill()` on an already-exited child raises ProcessLookupError that propagated to the harness's silent-BLOCKED handler — either way the task stranded with before_done_ran_at stamped, no verify, and an EMPTY escalation queue. Fix pattern (task 2090): (Layer A) spawn with start_new_session=True and on timeout SIGKILL the whole process group via os.killpg (guarded) + bounded reap; (Layer B) wrap the cross-unit run_fn call in run() with asyncio.wait_for(timeout=timeout_secs+grace) and file a born-at-L2 infra_issue via _file_infra_issue_and_block on TimeoutError OR any Exception — an unconditional backstop that guarantees an escalation even if the subprocess is unkillable/detached (before_done_ran_at already stamped => safe, no re-run). Note _default_inspect_unit still has the same unbounded-communicate() risk (filed separately).

claim: Subprocess failure handling must be explicit, bounded, and regression-tested rather than relying on narrow exception assumptions or fragile timing defaults.

STEWARD TRIAGE RULE (dark-factory, measured 2026-09-04 on esc-4211-2): when a task's verify fails ONLY on tests it does not touch — inherited red from main — the commonly-suggested remedy "waive the known-inherited failures for this task's verify gate and let it land first" DOES NOT WORK in this repo, and a steward should not adopt it.

WHY. dark-factory-orchestrator.yaml:1118 sets `merge_verify_breadth: "full"`, so merge-role verify runs EVERY registered module's full suite, not just the touched modules. A waiver applied at the task-verify gate therefore buys nothing: the identical inherited failures re-fire at the MERGE gate, where the steward has no waiver to give. The two gates are not the same gate, and only the first one is waivable.

CORROBORATING SIGNAL, and the cheap way to detect this state: `git log --oneline main` and check whether any CODE commit has landed recently. During the 2026-09-03 deploy pause (config flip 731a0bafa9 at 16:57 flipping orchestrator_restart_on_merge_enabled true->false, which left 5 tests red on main), EVERY commit that landed on main for the following ~15 hours was docs/PRD-only. Docs commits clear because hooks/project-checks runs no pytest for them; code commits could not land at all. So "main has accepted only docs commits for hours" is a reliable fingerprint of a fleet-wide merge-gate closure from inherited red, not of a quiet queue.

WHAT TO DO INSTEAD. The only viable path is hold-then-rebase: hold the inheriting task, let the task that OWNS the red land, then rebase the lane onto the post-fix main and re-verify. Before escalating, convert the usual untested hypothesis ("it'll go green once X lands") into a MEASUREMENT you can cite — graft the owning task's fixed test file from its worktree into your own, run it against your unchanged base and source, then restore the single path with `git checkout -- <path>` and reconfirm a clean tree. On esc-4211-2 that turned 3-failed into 4-passed on task 4211's exact base in ~21s, which is far stronger evidence for the next handler than the inference it replaced.

CEILING NOTE: hold-then-rebase usually EXCEEDS the steward's ceiling, so plan to hand it off rather than wait. The steward watchdog is FLAT wall clock (1800s from session start) and polling does NOT reset it — unlike the idle-time watchdogs on architect/implementer/debugger/merger. A full-breadth verify plus review plus merge on the owning task will not fit. File the handoff at level=1 (which also pins the task against re-dispatch via QUEUE_HANDOFF) and close the L0 with action='close_only' — NOT 'resume', which would re-enter verify against the same unchanged base and reproduce the identical failures.

DO NOT, in this situation: edit the red test file (it is outside your task's scope and typically sits in the owning task's metadata.files under a live claim — a concurrent edit duplicates in-flight work and conflicts on merge), or revert the operator's config flip (a deliberate, measured ops action with its own owning task).

When a task branch is rebased or amended (e.g. a steward fixing a review escalation) AFTER its merge_request has already entered the orchestrator merge queue's frozen/verifying state, the in-flight verify keeps targeting the OLD frozen tip — skills/merge-queue/SKILL.md documents the frozen prefix as immutable, so newer commits are not picked up automatically. Detect this by comparing the merge worktree's HEAD parents (or get_merge_queue()'s two_layer_invariants field, which lists violation strings by request_id when non-empty, expected [] when healthy) against your current branch tip via `git merge-base --is-ancestor <your-latest-fix-sha> <frozen-merge-commit>`. Because merge_cancel has a known race with an active verify (see existing procedural_knowledge on 'sanctioned override of merge_cancel requires fixing the known cancel race with verify first'), a task-scoped agent should NOT call merge_cancel speculatively to fix a stale in-flight request it discovers mid-verify — escalate_blocker (category infra_issue) with the concrete commit-ancestry evidence instead, and let the steward/orchestrator decide whether to cancel+resubmit or confirm finalize re-validates against the live branch ref. Filed as esc-3115-3 for a concrete instance (task 3115, request mr-4178165a frozen on a commit that a mid-flight rebase had rewritten away entirely).

GOTCHA for a task agent RESUMING after an escalation whose handler resolution says "resume and proceed to verify/merge": that instruction addresses the PIPELINE, not you. Do NOT reach for `mcp__plan-tools__report_ready_to_merge` to act on it. That tool is scoped to an ARCHITECT discovering a merge-landing desync during verify-premises, and its own docstring rules out the resuming-implementer case twice: it requires (a) main to be an ANCESTOR of the branch tip, and (b) verify AND review to have already passed on THAT EXACT TIP. After a steward amends the branch to clear a blocking review finding, (b) is false by construction — the last verify predates the steward's fix commit, which is now the tip. And (a) is usually false too, because main advances while the escalation sits (measured on task 5021: branch merge-base e29d7618 vs main tip 5e3ddf15ae, i.e. diverged, needing the harness's pre-verify rebase). Calling it anyway costs nothing at the orchestrator — it re-validates the desync predicate first-hand and does not trust the report — but it is a mis-signal and wastes a turn.

WHAT TO DO INSTEAD when every plan step already shows status=done: re-verify the tree yourself (run the task's own test module + ruff in the WORKTREE's venv), confirm `git status` is clean and `git diff main...HEAD --stat` still touches only the plan's declared files, then simply END YOUR TURN. There is no "I'm finished" tool for an implementer with a fully-done plan — the orchestrator routes the task onward on its own.

RELATED, and the thing that makes a resumed plan look broken when it is not: if the harness rebased the branch (the iteration log records e.g. "Rebased onto main (8a40be86 -> e29d7618)"), EVERY commit SHA recorded in plan.json's steps is stale and `git merge-base --is-ancestor <recorded_sha> HEAD` returns non-zero for ALL of them. That is expected post-rebase bookkeeping drift, NOT missing work — verify content survival by reading `git log --oneline <merge-base>..HEAD` and matching commit subjects to steps, never by checking recorded SHAs for reachability.

claim: Before acting on a task’s verification or merge state, check the live pipeline conditions and use the role-appropriate route rather than assuming a waiver, update, or instruction applies.

members.text: In gui/sidecar/src/__tests__/session.test.ts, the shared test helpers are: drainStdinFirstLine (first stdin JSON line), waitForOutput (single matching outbound, event-driven), waitForOutputs (N matching outbounds, avoids side-effectful predicate), waitForStdinLines (wait until stdinLines.length >= N), makeMockProc(assistantContent[]) (EventEmitter+PassThrough trio + stdin accumulator + spawn mock, leaves stdout open). All four "hand-rolled mock subprocess" describe blocks (close-on-result race, stdin write error correlation, echoed tool_use_id validation, FIFO consumption) use makeMockProc to avoid boilerplate duplication.

In gui/sidecar/src/__tests__/session.test.ts the shared makeMockProc() helper emits its assistant event WITHOUT message.id. So every test built on it also triggers the one-shot degraded_turn_boundary notice, and since task 9067 every sidecar notice is mirrored to stderr via console.warn (SidecarSession.emitNotice). A test that counts console.warn calls must filter by its own message text, not use toHaveBeenCalledTimes on the bare spy.

Node gotcha (measured for task 9729, Node v22.23.4): a ChildProcess 'close' event fires only after the child's stdout has been read to EOF. If a test helper reads stdout through a paused async iterator (createLineReader / for-await over child.stdout) and stops after the line it wanted, any line the child prints afterwards stays buffered, so 'close' never fires and `await closed` hangs until the vitest timeout, with no exit code or stderr. Only a stdout with an empty buffer ends by itself. Before awaiting 'close', drain the rest of the iterator. gui/sidecar/src/__tests__/built-bundle.test.ts SidecarProcess.endInput() does this via drainOutbound(); a child that prints a second line on stdin EOF reproduced the hang (8 s timeout before the fix, 415 ms after).

claim: Sidecar subprocess tests must account for shared-helper side effects and drain stdout before awaiting child closure.

AMENDMENT-PASS PRECEDENT LADDER — a rung in the "frozen plan's prose about OBSERVATIONS is falsifiable" family (the standing rule recorded on the task-5637 rung, 4760a279; cf. 4486 and the task-5450 rung 4fdf44d0), with a FALSIFIER none of them carries: the claim was invalidated not by the runtime being different from what the architect believed, and not by a mislabelled step, but BY AN EARLIER STEP OF THE SAME PLAN — and that plan's own text had already anticipated the mechanism elsewhere. Task 5648, commits 4e8af43fc8 (step-6) and 1ec89ce503 (step-7).

THE CASE. Step-7 mandated a characterization guard — two `promote_to_l2` calls with one root_cause via `asyncio.gather` must yield exactly one L2 — and stated: "Assertion 2 passes today — it is the characterization guard that fails if step-8 ships the hop without the lock." Written at plan time that was true. But step-6 (hop `queue.make_id` off the loop at five write-path sites) had landed first, and its `await asyncio.to_thread(queue.make_id, ...)` sits BETWEEN `find_pending_l2_by_root_cause` and `queue.submit`. That new yield point is itself enough: under `gather` both coroutines' scans observe the pre-state and both mint. Measured, not reasoned — the guard was re-run against step-5's server.py (passed) and step-6's (failed, two 'created' L2s, esc-5648-1 and esc-5648-2).

WHY IT IS NOT A DEVIATION. Step-6's own frozen rationale already said "for `promote_to_l2` it sits inside the lock step-8 adds, so nothing else on this loop is in that region anyway." So the plan's DESIGN was coherent throughout; only step-7's present-tense bookkeeping sentence went stale between authoring and execution. Every step was implemented verbatim, nothing was re-sequenced, and no escalation was needed.

WHAT CHANGED IS WHAT THE TEST TESTIFIES TO, and that is the part worth a commit message. "Characterization guard against a hypothetical future mistake" and "live RED that the next step must close" are different claims about the same assertion, and a reviewer bisecting the branch meets the red one first.

THE CHEAP CHECK THIS GENERALIZES TO: when a plan step says a test "passes today", re-read the steps ALREADY LANDED for a yield point, lock, or ordering change they introduced into the same critical region — then run it. A plan is written against the base branch; by the time step N executes, steps 1..N-1 have moved the ground under every present-tense claim in it. The rule from 4760a279 holds unchanged (falsify OBSERVATION prose freely, treat DESIGN prose as binding); this names the commonest source of the falsification.

AMENDMENT-PASS PRECEDENT LADDER — a rung whose CONFLICT SOURCE is a frozen plan STEP's own clause list, and whose discriminator the ladder does not yet carry: OBEYING THE LITERAL TEXT WOULD HAVE MADE A LATER STEP'S RED PASS VACUOUSLY. Task 5601, commit 3f4170e5b5, esc-5601-3.

THE CASE. Step-14's text said "Add `_build_parser()` with `--root`, `--baseline`, `--json` and positional PATHs", while step-23/24 were the RED/GREEN pair that specify and implement `--json`. Declaring `--json` at step-14 makes argparse accept a flag whose verb runs --check instead — a flag that lies. Implementing it there instead steals step-24's work AND makes step-23's RED vacuous.

THE TEST THAT DECIDED IT, and it is new to the ladder: ask whether the literal reading damages a DOWNSTREAM step's ability to fail for the right reason. Every existing rung weighs the conflict inside the pass it occurs in. This one is decided by a later step's evidentiary value, so the fork is not "which reading is better here" but "which reading keeps the plan's own TDD instrument working". The step's headline (the --check verb) was completed in full; only the flag declaration moved to the step that implements it.

CORROBORATION FROM THE SAME SESSION, which is why this is worth recording as a test rather than an anecdote: the plan had ALREADY relied on exactly this reasoning once. Iteration 1's note explains that `shared` is imported bare, with no sys.path insert and no ImportError handling, specifically so step-25's RED is not vacuous. So "do not let an earlier step pre-satisfy a later RED" was already an operating principle of this plan; step-14 is the same principle applied to a clause the plan's own text did not think through.

A SECOND, DIFFERENT RUNG IN THE SAME TASK (esc-5601-4, commit 19511bb0c9): a frozen step said "CONFIRM the file is inside heuristic 14's ~1,500-line soft ceiling", and the measurement was 2,065 raw lines. A confirmation step whose predicate is FALSE cannot be discharged by confirming it. What was done instead: state the measurement (761 code lines, 46% prose), apply docs/code-quality.md's own "do not steer by raw line count" guidance, MEASURE both remedies before rejecting them (docstrings flat and non-redundant; a split would be the function-bags-over-shared-state shape heuristic 14 itself names as cheating), and record the reasoning in the module docstring rather than only in a commit message. Reading: when a plan step says "confirm X" and X is false, the step's real content is "measure X and account for it" — confirming it anyway is the only wrong answer.

Append a stamped peer under this topic; do not restate the ladder elsewhere.

Amendment-pass precedent, task 4486 (commits e37484b139 / 0a4b548c8c, esc-4486-1) — a fork shape the ladder does not yet name: the plan's stated CAUSAL PREMISE is falsified by measurement, while its INTENT is untouched. Distinct from the existing rungs, which all resolve a reviewer SUGGESTION against a frozen design_decision; here nobody disagreed with anybody, the plan simply asserted a fact about the runtime that is not true.

THE CASE. plan.json step-3 instructed: write a test that will be RED against step-2's bare `>>` append, because "under `set -euo pipefail` the failed redirection fails drain_check_verdict, which is always invoked via command substitution assigned to a plain variable, so the failure propagates out of the assignment and aborts the whole script. Confirm that is the observed RED before writing step-4." Design decision 6 carried the same claim. The test arrived GREEN on first run. Measured (bash 5.2.21): the abort happens only when the failing write is the function's LAST command; step-2 had deliberately placed the contractual `printf` last, so the mid-body failure never reached the assignment. The call-site half of the plan's reasoning was correct; the position half was missing.

THE TEST THAT DECIDED IT. Separate the plan's FACTUAL CLAIM from the PROPERTY it was invoked to protect, and ask whether the property still wants protecting once the claim is gone. Here the claim ("this aborts today") was false, but the property ("a mis-typed operator trace path must never cost the redeploy") was real, still unpinned, and cheap to enforce — and measurement showed the guard IS the difference between abort and survival in the last-command configuration. So: apply the step as written, keep the test, and rewrite every piece of prose that repeated the false claim.

THE RESOLUTION, three parts, all required.
1. APPLY the step's code unchanged. A falsified premise is not automatically a dead step; re-derive the step's value from the property, not from the premise.
2. NEVER copy the plan's causal sentence into the source comment or the test docstring. plan.json stays frozen with the false claim in it, so a comment repeating it verbatim would enshrine a statement the same branch disproves — the exact drift the repo's comment stance warns about. Write what was MEASURED instead, and say plainly that the guard is redundant with today's ordering and exists so the property survives a reorder. A reader who finds a guard that provably changes nothing, with a comment claiming it prevents catastrophe, correctly concludes the code is confused.
3. FILE escalate_info with the measurements as structured `evidence`, and repeat the reasoning in the commit message. Without it, a reviewer diffing plan.json against the landed code sees a step that promised RED, a test that was born GREEN, and a guard with no failing case — three unexplained mismatches.

GENERALIZATION: when a plan tells you to "confirm the RED before proceeding", that instruction is load-bearing and the confirmation can FAIL. Treat a GREEN-on-arrival RED step as a finding to measure and report, not as a step to quietly skip or as a test to bend until it fails.

Amendment-pass precedent, task 4354 (commits e9b317d471 / c2802fbc17) — a rung with a conflict shape none of the existing ones has: the fork was INTERNAL TO THE FROZEN PLAN, with no reviewer involved, and one side of it was not merely worse but physically unexecutable.

THE CASE. Plan step-9 said: delete `_DATACLASS_DOUBLE_DEBT` from fused-memory/scripts/check_bare_magicmock_config.py, and "leave every other symbol alone in THIS step; the rest of the machinery is step-10's". Plan step-10 then claimed for itself the removal of that dict's only two references — the `_debt_budget(filename, _DATACLASS_DOUBLE_DEBT)` lookup and the Rule B `_apply_debt_budget(...)` block inside `find_violations`. A deleted name cannot remain referenced: obeying both would make `find_violations` raise NameError on its first call.

THE TEST THAT DECIDED IT — read the step's own CONFIRM clause as the arbiter, not its prose. Step-9's CONFIRM RED predicted "the gate fails with exactly 2 plain Rule B violations" and "(b) and (c) should already PASS, since the dict is gone". Both require `find_violations` to RUN. So the step's verification clause proves which of its own two sentences is load-bearing: the deletion, not the leave-everything-else. The call sites moved into step-9; step-10 kept everything else it was assigned. Measured after step-9: exactly 2 failed / 143 passed, the predicted shape to the site.

A SECOND ARBITER IN THE SAME STEP. Step-9's CONFIRM also said "(a) FAILS — both attributes still exist", which reads as contradicting "the dict is gone" three lines above. It does not: assertion (a) covered TWO symbols, and only the second (`_debt_overrun_msg`, deleted in step-10) survived step-9, so (a) failed for a real reason. When a CONFIRM clause looks self-contradictory, check whether it is asserting a conjunction before concluding the plan is wrong.

GENERAL RULE THIS YIELDS. When a plan assigns a constant's deletion to step N and its call sites to step N+1, the call sites move to step N — always. There is no version of that split that leaves an importable module. Do the forced minimum (delete the lookup, replace the guarded extend with the plain one), leave every genuinely optional part of step N+1 alone, and file an escalate_info naming the moved lines so a reviewer diffing plan.json against the commits does not read it as scope slip. Filed as esc-4354-5; the rationale is also repeated in the commit message, per the rung-2 (task 3890) reflex.

Related: esc-4354-4 in the same task is a different failure — the task's own DONE-WHEN named `_is_debt_path` / `_find_dataclass_double_violations`, symbols task 4246 had renamed AND shared with another rule, so a literal reading would have deleted a live baseline. Naming drift in the TASK and an unexecutable split in the PLAN are separate defects that can both appear in one task.

AMENDMENT-PASS PRECEDENT LADDER — a rung in the "conflict INTERNAL to one frozen plan step" family (cf. the task-3193 and task-5xxx rungs), with a discriminator none of them carries: THE STEP'S TWO HALVES ARE OF DIFFERENT KINDS — a PERFORMANCE MECHANISM and a DESIGN INVARIANT — and the resolution was that the fork was a FALSE DILEMMA. Task 5705, esc-5705-1, commit 367a436969.

THE CASE. Plan step-6 prescribed a mechanism: "Build a Set of surviving `path` values per project key so the scan is O(rows x lock_set) rather than O(rows x modules)". Its own CLOSING SENTENCE prescribed an invariant: "Keep `rowTouchesModule` exported: it is the single source of the membership rule that `cellStateFor` will delegate to in step-12" — restating design decision 5, whose rationale is that duplicating the cross-project rule "would put [it] in two files and let the axis filter drift from the cell renderer". The two conflict: a per-PROJECT path Set encodes the project check AS ITS GROUPING KEY, and must also reproduce both falsy-project allowances, so the mechanism makes the module a second source of the very rule the invariant single-sources.

THE RESOLUTION, AND WHY IT IS NOT A RUNG-1 PICK. Rung 1 (task 4705) applies when the text OFFERS alternatives and you choose the non-conflicting one. Here nothing was offered — the step named one mechanism. But the mechanism's stated PURPOSE was a complexity bound, not a data structure, and a DIFFERENT index satisfies the bound without touching the invariant: key the Map by module PATH, and decide each hit by calling the exported predicate itself. O(rows x lock_set) exactly as specified (the step's own "~13k probes, versus 12.9M" holds verbatim); the index carries no copy of the rule.

THE TEST THAT DECIDES IT. When one frozen step's two halves conflict, FIRST ask whether each half states a PURPOSE or a MECHANISM. A mechanism is only ever instrumental — it is evidence of what the author wanted, not the want itself. If a third spelling satisfies the stated purpose of one half AND the invariant of the other, neither half loses and there is nothing to adjudicate. Only if no such spelling exists do you rank the halves (correctness over performance, invariant over mechanism) and fall to rung 2 or 3.

DISPOSITION: applied in full, escalate_info filed (rung-2 discipline — the frozen plan text keeps saying "Set ... per project key", so a reviewer diffing plan against code sees an unexplained mismatch otherwise), and the reasoning repeated in the commit message. Both cross-project regression cases pass.

GENERALISATION WORTH KEEPING: a plan step that specifies a DATA STRUCTURE alongside a complexity target is over-specified, and the complexity target is the part that was actually reasoned about. Treat the structure as the author's first draft of a means, not as a constraint — but say so out loud, because only the frozen text survives into review.

AMENDMENT-PASS PRECEDENT LADDER — a rung whose CONFLICT SOURCE is new: a FROZEN PLAN STEP contradicting the TASK DESCRIPTION'S OWN RATIFIED TEXT, adjudicated by a steward on an implementer-filed design_concern rather than by the implementer mid-pass. Task 5374, esc-5374-1, commit ad105996f6.

THE CASE. Task 5374 writes a shadow-mode measurement for L2 adjudication. Its description carries a skeleton ratified by Leo (ruling D8) with two lists: the human-forever gates ("...every `milestone_gate` and `orchestrator-deterministic` record") and four first-tranche classes to shadow, one of which is `design_concern_semantic_collision`. Plan steps 3/4 specified `mechanically_gated` to return a gate slug for EVERY member of `escalation.authority.L2_AUTO_CLOSE_DENY_CATEGORIES` — a set that contains `design_concern`. Steps 5/6 exclude every gated record from all rates. So the frozen plan instructed the session to stamp a class whose every stamp the same plan's counter discards: the class could never reach its own "95% or better over at least 10 items" adoption threshold. The implementer implemented the plan verbatim, filed the tension as a design_concern with the measurement attached, and explicitly did NOT change the frozen step.

THE TEST THAT DECIDED IT — ASK WHAT QUESTION EACH TABLE ANSWERS, not which set is bigger. `L2_AUTO_CLOSE_DENY_CATEGORIES` answers "may the AUTO-WATCHER IDENTITY auto-close this at L2?"; its own module docstring scopes it to the identified callers in `ROLE_LEVEL_ALLOWLIST`, whose sole member is the auto-watcher. The detector answers "does the ratified gate list keep this record with the human FOREVER?". The two overlap on the runner-filed categories and diverge on exactly one member. Binding the second question to the first table's answer is the defect; the remedy is a DERIVED set (denylist minus the one named member) so new runner-filed categories still propagate for free and a hand-written literal still fails the SPOT guard.

THREE INDEPENDENT WITNESSES made this an adjudication rather than a judgement call, and finding a second and third is what converts "the plan is arguably wrong" into "the plan is wrong":
1. The ratified text itself names the mechanical gates and `design_concern` is not among them.
2. `HUMAN_FOREVER_GATES` in the shipped code — pinned to the policy document by a doc-contract test — has no `design_concern` member.
3. BOTH prose documents the task wrote (`docs/escalation-standing-policy.md` and `skills/escalation-watcher/SKILL.md`) already described the detector as covering exactly a `milestone_gate` category and the `orchestrator-deterministic` role. The CODE was the outlier, not the prose — so the fix removed a contradiction rather than choosing between two defensible readings.

THE GENERAL RULE THIS RUNG ADDS. A frozen plan step does not outrank the task description it was planned from. When a plan step and the task's ratified text disagree, the ratified text wins and the plan step is amended — this is NOT the rung-2 (task 3890) "conflicts with the literal text but preserves the rationale" case, because there is no rationale to preserve: the plan step was derived from a misreading of which table to bind to. Record the deviation in the commit message and in the module, and re-measure the defect on the tree BEFORE changing anything (here: `mechanically_gated(<category='design_concern'>)` returned `'milestone_gate'` — a slug that is additionally false about such a record).

ALSO A RUNG ABOUT WHO RULES. The implementer was right to implement verbatim and escalate rather than amend: the fix crosses a plan step, and an implementer amending a frozen step on its own authority is the failure mode the ladder exists to prevent. The steward adjudicating a filed design_concern is the cheap, reversible, in-band path — and it was safe to take without Leo precisely because the ratified text already answered the question and the change grants no authority (`authority.py` untouched; the auto-watcher still  [cut]

AMENDMENT-PASS PRECEDENT LADDER — a rung whose CONFLICT SOURCE is new: not a reviewer suggestion, not a frozen design_decision, and not a fresh measurement about the step's output, but the PLAN'S OWN STEP/COMMIT GRANULARITY colliding with a repo GATE that makes the planned intermediate commit unlandable. Task 5097, commit 04d61e23c4.

THE CASE. The plan put a signature change (step-6: add a required keyword-only `policy` to HostAllocator.acquire, plus its test-file call-site fallout) and the production wiring (step-7: merge_queue.py's call site + two harness call sites) in separate steps, and the standing implementer instruction is one commit per step. Measured after step-6 alone: pyright reported exactly 3 `reportCallIssue: Argument missing for parameter "policy"` errors, at precisely the 3 sites step-7 was to fix. hooks/project-checks runs pyright per staged package and fails the commit, so a step-6-only commit could not land without --no-verify.

THE TEST THAT DECIDED IT — and it is the rung-2 (task 3890) test applied to a non-design-decision conflict source. Ask whether the plan's STATED RATIONALE survives the deviation. Here it does not merely survive, it REQUIRES it: step-6's own design decision chose "required rather than defaulted" precisely because it "makes a missing `policy=` a reportCallIssue error on every pre-commit and every verify ... in place of the test the gate forbids". The gate that blocks the intermediate commit IS the enforcement the plan asked for. Splitting the commits would have meant defeating the rationale (--no-verify) to honour the granularity; combining honours the rationale and deviates only on commit boundaries, which no design decision names.

GENERALISATION. When the conflict is with a MECHANICAL GATE rather than a stated decision, the discriminator is whether the plan's rationale INVOKES that gate. If it does, the gate's behaviour is inside the plan's intent and you follow the gate. If it does not, treat it as an ordinary rung-2/rung-3 fork.

ALTERNATIVE REJECTED, and why it is worth naming: keeping two commits by pre-wiring the production call site to a hardcoded `policy='prefer_local'` in the earlier commit. It type-checks and is behaviourally identical to the default, so it LOOKS free — but it lands a commit in which production ignores the operator's config, and it edits a zero-slack ratchet file twice, doubling the line-neutrality exposure for no gain. Prefer combining over manufacturing a green-but-semantically-wrong intermediate state.

RESOLUTION SHAPE (same as rung 2): apply in full, file escalate_info recording the deviation with the raw measurements (esc-5097-10), mark BOTH plan steps done at the single SHA, and repeat the reasoning in the commit message so a reviewer never has to guess whether the combination was an oversight.

AMENDMENT-PASS PRECEDENT LADDER — a rung whose CONFLICT SOURCE is two FROZEN PLAN STEPS contradicting each other about the same field, discovered only when the later step's GREEN turned the earlier step's GREEN red. The existing "conflict INTERNAL to one frozen plan step" rungs (task 3193, and the 2026-09-20 both-halves-correctness rung) cover one step disagreeing with itself; this is two steps, both already implemented and committed, disagreeing across a step boundary.

THE CASE. Task 5587, commit 98168f2f79. Step 3(h) required a degraded census Datum's `reason` to be the `CensusVocabularyError` message "verbatim" — written and committed as an equality assertion. Step 6 then required an UNKNOWN datum's reason to "name which case" it was (no previous value vs. a last-good past the retention bound), and step 5(f) required the retention bound to be READABLE OUT of the reason. Implementing step 6 by appending a disposition clause uniformly broke step 3(h)'s equality assertion. Both step specs were frozen; neither could simply be dropped.

THE TEST THAT DECIDED IT. Ask whether the two requirements are in conflict on EVERY cell or only on their OVERLAP, then look for a partition of the cells on which each requirement governs alone. Here the cells are the two UNKNOWN sub-cases. Appending only when a last good was DISCARDED leaves the no-previous-value cell verbatim (step 3(h) holds, on the path `CensusVocabularyError` actually travels) and the past-retention cell annotated (step 5(f) holds). No cell is governed by both. The tie-break for WHICH cell gets the exception was not arbitrary: a discarded value is a fact the consumer cannot otherwise account for — it saw that census a minute ago and needs to know why it is gone — whereas a value that never existed needs no such account.

WHY IT IS A RUNG AND NOT JUST A BUG FIX. The reflex is to relax the earlier test to a substring match, which is the move that makes a frozen requirement quietly weaker and is exactly what the ladder exists to catch. Note too that a third, already-LANDED source outranked both plan steps and decided which requirement was the stronger: `census.py::CensusVocabularyError`'s own docstring says the access layer serves "this message verbatim as its `reason`". A frozen plan step in tension with a dependency's shipped contract loses to the contract.

GENERALISATION. When two frozen steps collide, do not pick a winner before enumerating the cells each one actually names. A partition often exists, and it is usually the better design than either uniform reading — here the resulting rule ("verbatim is the default, the clause is the exception") reads as a deliberate policy rather than as a compromise.

claim: When frozen plans conflict with evidence, dependencies, or gates, measure the issue, preserve the underlying intent and invariants, and document any justified deviation.

members.text: git 2.43.0 `git merge-tree --write-tree --name-only <base> <head>` (the object-store-only conflict probe for the two-layer merge queue, git_ops.merge_tree_conflicts): exit code 0 = clean (stdout is just the merged tree OID on line 0); exit code 1 = conflict (stdout = OID line, then deduplicated conflicted paths one-per-line, then a BLANK line, then informational messages like "Auto-merging f"/"CONFLICT (content)..."); exit 128 = bad/unknown rev. To extract conflicted_paths: split stdout, drop line 0 (OID), collect lines until the first blank line (that blank line separates the "Conflicted file info" section from the "informational messages" section). It writes only loose objects — no worktree/index/ref mutation — so it is safe to call many times per tick at cwd=project_root.

`git merge-tree --write-tree main task/<id>` deterministically REPRODUCES a merge-phase thrash offline, without touching the worktree, without a merge-queue submission, and without needing merge_status to resolve. On dark-factory task 3464 (2026-08-05) it took one command to turn an UNCONFIRMED skew hypothesis into an exact diagnosis: it printed the conflicting path and the conflict count, revealing a single conflict hunk in scripts/tests/test_legibility_inventory.py.

This is the right FIRST move when an escalation reports merge thrash with `merge_status` unavailable (state=unknown), because it needs neither the merge queue nor the escalation server. It also directly answers the flake-vs-real question: if merge-tree reproduces the conflict, the failure is DETERMINISTIC and must not be recorded as a flake. That is exactly why the thrash guard saw an identical `merge_outcome_signature` (a9e3cc533c2ae7fa) on both attempts — a deterministic content conflict produces a stable signature, so `consecutive_merge_thrash=2` was the guard working correctly, not noise.

Follow-up: `git show <merge-tree-output-tree>:<path>` piped through a grep for conflict markers enumerates the hunks in the merged tree, so the size of the resolution is known BEFORE committing to a remediation option.

claim: Use `git merge-tree --write-tree` first to safely reproduce and diagnose merge conflicts offline, without modifying the worktree or relying on merge-queue status.

members.text: Merge-lane production-code gotcha (task 8523): anything new in worker.py::SpeculativeMergeWorker::_run_inflight_verify that reads the verify task's result right after `out = verify_task.result()` (before the chain/ordinary arms split) must not assume a MergeOutcome. The deep-dispatch and deep-integration-gate test scenes hand a bare VerifyResult through a patched _run_post_merge_verify, and only `out is None` is safe there. Task 8523's telemetry hook read `out.verify_skipped` and turned 7 tests red in test_merge_queue_deep_dispatch.py and test_merge_queue_deep_integration_gate.py; the fix was `isinstance(out, MergeOutcome) and out.verify_skipped`. Run both files after touching that spot.

GOTCHA (dark-factory merge lane, since task 8526): SpeculativeMergeWorker._dispatch_item no longer calls _run_inflight_verify when it launches a verify. It passes a functools.partial to _verify_releasing_at_verdict, which calls it inside the new verify task, so a cancel before the task starts leaves no never-awaited coroutine. A test that mocks worker._run_inflight_verify and asserts assert_called_once() right after `await worker._dispatch_item(item)` sees 0 calls. Await entry.verify_task first, after narrowing with isinstance(entry, InflightEntry), because _dispatch_item can return NoHost. If the entry lands behind another, its verdict also awaits host_allocator.release(lease), so a MagicMock allocator needs `release = AsyncMock()`. A related change: a released verdict frees its host, so a cascade test that expects runner.cancel_verify on a follower must keep the follower's verify gated until the cancel has happened.

Gotcha (dark-factory merge lane, measured while planning task 8523, 2026-11-05): SpeculativeMergeWorker._teardown_verify_task is called at two nested levels. The cascade, the stop() drains and tip adoption cancel the OUTER _run_inflight_verify task, and its finally orphan guard then reaps the INNER verify (lease=None); the _run_verify_reaped partials (gate on head host, train host) are also reaps reacting to an outer cancel. Anything recorded per cancel must be emitted only by the deliberate canceller, or every cascade is double-counted. Also, _emit_speculative str()-ifies every data value, so nested/structured event fields must bypass it.

claim: When changing speculative-merge verification, respect its task and outcome boundaries, and test the real async lifecycle to avoid brittle assumptions and duplicate effects.

members.text: In dark-factory, ruff's isort (rule I001) treats sibling workspace packages as THIRD-PARTY from inside another member. No member declares `known-first-party`, so isort infers first-party from `src`: inside orchestrator/, `orchestrator` resolves via orchestrator/src/orchestrator and is first-party, while `escalation`/`shared` are third-party. A function-scope lazy-import block mixing them (e.g. `from escalation.models import Escalation` then `from orchestrator.foo import X`) looks alphabetically sorted but trips I001 — the two lines are in different isort sections and need a blank line between them. Confirm the exact fix with `uv run ruff check --diff <file>` before editing.

In the fused-memory package, ruff-isort classifies `shared.*` imports as THIRD-PARTY, not first-party: fused-memory/pyproject.toml sets no isort known-first-party or src config, and `shared` is an installed dependency. So `from shared.X import Y` must sit in the SAME import block as `pytest` with no blank line between them — inserting a separator splits one group in two and trips I001 ("Import block is un-sorted or un-formatted"). Run `uv run ruff check --diff <file>` to see the exact intended fix before editing imports by hand.

Gotcha (task 3118, orchestrator): when adding a `shared.*` import to an orchestrator module, ruff's isort (I001) classifies `shared` / `escalation` / `fused_memory` as THIRD-PARTY, while only `orchestrator` is first-party — so `from shared.invocation_outcome import ...` must be placed BEFORE the `from orchestrator.* import ...` block, not after it (same rule inside `if TYPE_CHECKING:` blocks and function-local import blocks). Placing the shared import next to a related orchestrator import — the intuitive grouping, especially when each carries an explanatory comment — trips I001. `ruff check --diff <file>` shows the intended reordering; `--fix` moves each comment with its import.

Why this bites specifically on task branches: hooks/pre-commit runs the ruff+pyright project-checks ONLY on branch==main, so task-branch commits are not lint-gated at all (19 consecutive commits landed with 6 I001 errors before anything noticed). An implementer must run lint/type manually before declaring a task done. In a pooled worktree lane where `uv run` is broken by the EXDEV fault, use the main-checkout venv directly: `/home/leo/src/dark-factory/.venv/bin/python -m ruff check <files>` (needs no build step), and for types `cd <worktree>/orchestrator && /home/leo/src/dark-factory/.venv/bin/pyright` — orchestrator's [tool.pyright] extraPaths are RELATIVE (`../shared/src` etc.), so running it from the worktree's own package dir correctly resolves the worktree copies rather than the main checkout.

In shared/tests, sibling test-helper modules imported by bare name (e.g. `from _capacity_skip import ...`, `from _usage_gate_test_helpers import ...`, resolved via conftest.py's sys.path prepend) are classified by ruff's isort as THIRD-PARTY, not first-party. So they must sit in the same import block as `pytest` with NO blank line between them; only `from shared.* import ...` gets its own first-party block. Putting a blank line before the bare-name helper import trips ruff I001 ("Import block is un-sorted"). This bites when extracting a new shared test helper module — `ruff check --fix` resolves it.

Gotcha (dark-factory ruff I001): within a workspace member like orchestrator, sibling workspace packages (escalation.*, shared.*, fused_memory.*) are classified THIRD-PARTY by ruff's isort — they resolve from the shared .venv — while only orchestrator.* is first-party. A mixed import block therefore needs a blank-line group separator between them. This bites most often on FUNCTION-LOCAL import blocks inside a test, where the grouping is easy to overlook; the module header of orchestrator/tests/test_workflow_e2e.py shows the same split. Check with `ruff check --select I --diff <file>`, which prints exactly where the blank line goes.

In dashboard/pyproject.toml, [tool.ruff.lint] has no isort known-first-party setting, so ruff treats `shared.*` imports (the sibling shared/src/shared package) as third-party, not first-party. Convention (matches app.py, scheduler.py, redux_api.py): `from shared.X import Y` must be grouped with third-party imports (alphabetically among httpx/pytest/etc, above the blank line), while `from dashboard.*` imports form the separate first-party group below. Placing a new `shared.*` import in the dashboard-imports group trips ruff's I001. Fix with `ruff check --fix <file>` — safe, mechanical, matches the tool's own suggested diff.

claim: Ruff isort groups imports by configured classification, not project intuition; follow its third-party/first-party boundaries and check `ruff check --diff` before editing.
