Reify testing technique — how to pin a constraint that GENUINELY must live in a trait body. The known gotcha (memories 06e35691, eea5b075, 10c6eb04) says a bare trait body is not dimension-checked, so rewrite the probe as a `structure`. That works for breadth pins, but not when the stdlib site under test IS a trait and the trait-ness is the point (structural_physical.ri `trait Physical { constraint material.density > 0kg/m^3 }`, materials_electrical.ri `trait Insulating { constraint dielectric_strength > 0.0V/m }`). For those, drop to EVAL level: `reify_test_support::check_source_with_stdlib` (needs reify-eval's existing `eval-helpers` dev-dep feature; no Cargo.toml change), declare the trait plus a conforming structure, and assert `reify_ir::Satisfaction::Satisfied` on every injected constraint result — plus a non-empty check so a conformer that injected nothing cannot pass vacuously, and a paired `Violated` case on a value that genuinely fails the bound. Assert the Satisfaction VALUE, never "no error": a regressed dimension coercion makes `eval_cmp` compare Scalar-vs-Real and degrade SILENTLY to `Indeterminate` + a ConstraintIndeterminate warning rather than erroring, so only an equality assertion converts that into a test failure. Worked example: crates/reify-eval/tests/polymorphic_zero_trait_eval.rs (task 6038, 3 pins).

Reify trait-body checking is DEFERRED to conformance: a `trait` compiled with NO conforming structure emits ZERO error diagnostics no matter how broken its body is — dimension-mismatched constraints, references to undefined member fields, and wrong `let` type annotations all pass silently. Adding a conformer (`structure def C : T { ... }`) makes all three fire (`DimensionMismatch`, `StructureMemberNotFound`, `TypeMismatchForTraitMember` respectively). Consequence: an absence-of-diagnostic assertion (`assert_no_error_diagnostics` / `assert_no_diagnostics`) written against a bare trait body is VACUOUS — it passes regardless of what the compiler does. The vacuity condition is precisely "trait body with no conformer", NOT "trait body". Measured on main @ 6927f3c0db (task 6143); pinned in crates/reify-compiler/tests/harness_traits/trait_body_deferred_check_tests.rs.

claim: Trait bodies are checked only when a conformer exists, so absence-of-diagnostic tests on bare traits are vacuous; include a conformer to test compile-time behavior.

members.text: Guard tests in tests/scripts/ that sweep the repo for a literal token (e.g. `git grep 'skills/'` over all test files) may assert that NEW hits are triaged into a known set, but must NOT assert that an exclusion-set entry still matches. The "stale exclusion" direction turns comments and docstrings in unrelated packages into a load-bearing merge gate: a cosmetic reword that drops the literal substring red-walls the guard from another package's diff, with a failure message about a decision the editing author has no context for. Unmatched exclusion keys are inert (membership is only ever consulted for the new-hit direction), so deletion is safe; prune stale entries opportunistically when the file is next touched. A word-boundary or regex variant is NOT a fix — it keeps the same prose coupling while hiding it. (Task 3554 review finding, 2026-08-06.)

SIGHTING + NUANCE under topic `guard-tests-grep-code-not-prose` (task 3226, review cycle 2, blocking): the prose-vs-code rule bites even when a guard scans its OWN module's source, not another file's. `tests/scripts/test_check_lock_charter_drift.py::test_module_import_resolves_no_checkout_at_module_scope` did `src = Path(drift.__file__).read_text()` and failed on any column-0 line containing `resolve_reify_checkout(`. Because `src.splitlines()` includes the module docstring and that docstring's lines ARE at column 0, and because the module's prose necessarily EXPLAINS the very construct being banned, rewording the docstring — changing zero code — turned it red. Self-ownership does not rescue a text scan; if anything it guarantees the false positive, since the rationale and the banned token are the same string.

THE EXECUTABLE DISCRIMINATOR (use this to classify any suspected prose-pin, and to confirm a fix): insert a column-0 line naming the banned construct INTO the module docstring, change no code, and run the guard. Red => it is a prose/comment-content pin. Green => it is referential integrity. This is a two-line diff and settles the question without argument.

AST FORM PASSES THE DISCRIMINATOR — measured, not assumed. Two sibling guards in the same file (`test_source_contains_no_parents_index_arithmetic`, `test_no_ambient_environ_reread`) route through an `ast.parse()` helper instead of `read_text()`. Injecting column-0 docstring prose naming `Path(__file__).parents[5]` and `os.environ` left both GREEN (2 passed). A resume briefing had asserted these two carried the same defect; running the discriminator showed they do not. So: when a structural guard must ban a construct the module's own docs discuss, `ast.parse` + `ast.walk` is the fix, and it is also strictly stronger (it catches `x.parents [3]` and an aliased `par = p.parents; par[3]`).

DELETION IS OFTEN THE RIGHT FIX, BUT VERIFY THE CLAIMED REPLACEMENT COVERAGE FIRST. The 3226 review justified deleting the scan by claiming a sibling subprocess-import assertion already covered the invariant. Tested: it does NOT — a genuine module-scope `resolve_reify_checkout(...)` call leaves that subprocess import PASSING, because the function returns rather than raising. The real cover was elsewhere (`TestResolve`'s cases set the env var AFTER import, so they detect the actual harm — an un-steerable import-frozen answer; freezing the answer in a module-scope constant reds six of them). Confirm the replacement coverage by construction before deleting, and cite the case that actually holds the line, not the one that looks adjacent.

STAMPED PEER under topic `guard-tests-grep-code-not-prose` (task 5088 review; complements the 3554 canonical and the 3781/3817/4064/4361 "delete prose-pinning meta-tests" cluster). NEW ANGLE not covered by those: the prose pin was CREATED BY an attempt to soften a VALUE pin on an operator lever.

THE TRAP. A test pinned `orchestrator_restart_on_merge_enabled: true` in dark-factory-orchestrator.yaml. On 2026-09-03 the operator deliberately flipped it to `false` (the fleet deploy pause), which reddened main. The tempting repair — the one that shipped and was then rejected in review — was to relax the assertion to "`true`, OR `false` AND a `DEPLOY PAUSE — TEMPORARY` marker appears in the contiguous comment block above the key." That converted a wrong-but-honest value pin into a prose pin, and inherited both halves of the prose defect: rewording the comment with identical declared intent (a hyphen instead of the U+2014 em dash) turns it red, while ANY comment carrying the magic phrase — including one copy-pasted forward from a pause lifted long ago — turns it green. It can check the string's shape, never its truth. Adding a `pytest.raises(AssertionError)` meta-test proving the relaxed guard "still bites" does not rescue it; it just tests the substring match harder.

THE RULE. Do not write a test that pins the VALUE of a config key the operator is expected to change. An operator flipping an ops lever is not a code defect — it is the mechanism working. When such a test goes red because the operator acted, DELETE it; do not relax it into matching the justification comment, and do not relocate the marker into a machine-readable YAML key either (that makes the assertion executable but still pins a lever).

WHAT TO KEEP INSTEAD. The value-agnostic DRIFT guards in the same file survived review intact and are what the "silent drift" rationale actually rests on: the YAML key still exists, the same-named pydantic field still exists, and `parsed == raw`. Under pydantic `extra='ignore'` a key typo or a `config.py` field rename silently reverts to the field default with no error anywhere, and only those catch it. Note the equality term alone is vacuous whenever the committed value happens to equal the field default — say so in the docstring rather than letting a reader assume it is doing work it is not.

AFTERCARE. Deleting a pin usually orphans cross-references: two docstrings in a sibling test file still read "deploy policy is pinned by <the gutted file>, not here." A dangling pointer to a deleted guard is worse than none — the next reader follows it, finds nothing, assumes a bad merge, and reinstates the pin. Name the absence as deliberate ("pinned by NO test — operator lever; task 5020 is the gate"), and mirror that sentence into the task that will perform the change.

STAMPED PEER under topic `guard-tests-grep-code-not-prose` (task 5247, amendment pass, commit 780ac5c9): WHEN a stale-exclusion assertion IS legitimate — the distinction is FILE-scoped vs HIT-scoped exclusions, and the canonical's "unmatched exclusion keys are inert" holds only for the latter.

THE CANONICAL'S RULE, unchanged: gate only the ADD direction; a stale key in a HIT-scoped exclusion set (one that enumerates known individual matches) is inert, so prune opportunistically rather than enforcing freshness with a test. Task 3554's ratchet is the case that established it: a cosmetic reword in a file the guard does not own red-walled an unrelated merge gate.

THE CASE THAT REFINES IT. tests/scripts/test_reify_closure_staleness_sweep_retired.py sweeps the tracked tree for two retired PATH tokens and exempts files by REPO-RELATIVE PATH, each with a written reason. That exclusion is FILE-scoped: the key removes the whole file from the sweep, permanently. So when a file's last retired-token mention is later edited away, the stale key is NOT inert — it is a hole. The file keeps its exemption and is then silently free to reintroduce a live reference to the retired wiring, with the guard still green. Measured on this very branch: an earlier step re-pointed docs/prds/recurring-deterministic-tasks.capability-manifest.md so it no longer contained either token, and its allowlist entry had already outlived its subject before anyone noticed.

THE TEST. Ask what the exclusion key EXEMPTS. If it names a known hit (this line, this match), a stale key exempts nothing that still exists — inert, do not assert. If it names a FILE (or a directory, or any container), a stale key exempts everything that file might later contain — assert, because the exemption outlives its justification.

The in-repo precedent for the assert side is tests/scripts/test_atomic_write_regrowth.py::_ALLOWED_RENAMERS, whose `stale = set(_ALLOWED_RENAMERS) - actual; assert not stale` carries a comment saying it is a HARD assert kept rather than downgraded — same file-scoped shape (its keys are (path, symbol) sites).

NOT A LICENCE TO PIN PROSE. The canonical's primary rule is untouched: what is matched here is two literal path/unit-name tokens (`consume_redispatch_requests`, `reify-closure-staleness-sweep`), i.e. CODE identifiers that happen to appear inside documentation, never wording. A guard that asserted an allowlisted doc still SAYS something particular would be the banned shape, and an earlier iteration of this same module shipped exactly that (a substring-proximity check over doc prose) and was correctly rejected on review — see commit 733518914c.

NORM (task 3554, review-established): a guard/config test must never assert on comment or docstring PROSE in files it does not own. A ratchet in tests/scripts/ that required every entry of an exclusion set to still contain the literal 'skills/' made a cosmetic comment reword in scripts/tests/test_legibility_sampling.py red-wall a merge-blocking module config — measured as `1 failed, 5 passed` from a diff touching nothing the guard gated. Assert on RUNTIME state instead (discovered module-config prefixes, git ls-files/grep sweeps, parsed command targets, file existence). Do NOT "fix" such coupling with a word-boundary or regex variant: that keeps the identical cross-package prose dependency while hiding it. For a triage-style set (real-consumer inventory vs excluded mentions), gate only the ADD direction — an unmatched exclusion key is inert, since the untriaged check consults the triaged set for membership only, so a key matching no file cannot make any still-mentioning file pass. Prune stale exclusions opportunistically when the file is next touched.

THE REWORD TEST — the executable discriminator between a banned prose meta-test and a legitimate referential-integrity guard. Stamped peer under topic `guard-tests-grep-code-not-prose`, and a CORRECTION to mem0 ee434b90-4b4a-4b6c-b5e5-9e0cd3f2e7f1 ("Do NOT build, keep, or HARDEN tests that assert on docstring/comment PROSE"), which a task-4240 steward wrote on 2026-08-20 at the moment of its own self-reversal. That entry's CORE IS RIGHT (prose-wording pins are banned; hardening a docstring-pin regex is the specifically-banned remedy) but its CLASSIFICATION of task 4240's guard was wrong, and its claim that "main carries zero prose-asserting meta-tests in .py source" is misleading about what main actually carries.

THE TEST, applied on 2026-08-24: fully reword the sentence that carries the citation, keeping the identifier. A WORDING PIN goes red by definition. A REFERENTIAL-INTEGRITY guard stays green. Measured against task 4240's artifact on a scratch copy of main — rewriting dashboard/src/dashboard/app.py:453 end to end while keeping ``TestClient(app)`` left it at rc=0. Deleting the identifier gave rc=1. So the policy's own stated rationale clause "these tests lock cosmetic detail in place" is FALSIFIED against that artifact; it is not a wording pin.

TWO LANDED, UNCHALLENGED PRECEDENTS OF THE LEGITIMATE SHAPE (main, 2026-08-24):

WHAT THE POLICY ACTUALLY BANS, and where it is silent. roles.py ARCHITECT rule 5, roles.py REVIEWER_COMPREHENSIVE and triage.py's SKIP rules were all introduced by ONE commit, 7abff876d7 (2026-04-18, authored by Leo) — they are not three independent enforcement points, they share one premise. NONE asserts that an identifier resolves. The prose-vs-identifier distinction was drawn NOWHERE in roles.py, triage.py, CONTRIBUTING.md, CLAUDE.md, docs/ or plans/. GAP NOW CLOSED FOR THE REVIEWER ONLY (2026-08-24, commit 2ee2b5c569 — this clause REPLACES an earlier "As of 2026-08-24 Leo has NOT amended the text, so the exposure remains"). Leo approved a one-sentence carve-out appended to orchestrator/src/orchestrator/agents/roles.py::REVIEWER_COMPREHENSIVE: "NOT IN SCOPE: a check that a cited IDENTIFIER RESOLVES to a real symbol. The discriminator is executable — if fully rewording the surrounding sentence while keeping the identifier leaves the check green, it is referential integrity, not a wording pin." members.text: The commit_planning manifest-stamping machinery (task 2578) confirmed working end-to-end at full batch scale on 2026-07-30 (server-side-api-error-handling batch, 15 tasks): the single bulk commit_planning call stamped 15/15 Greek labels with real task ids (no missing_labels, no errors), copied ONLY mechanical (grep) delivered_checks into producer metadata.delivered_checks (manual-kind checks correctly stayed sidecar-only, e.g. task 3319 got exactly its 3 grep checks and none of its 1 manual), and REWROTE the sidecar YAML in normalized form (unquoted strings, 2-space lists, folded long lines — a ~364-insertion/301-deletion diff on a 15-task file). Don't be surprised by the reformat; commit the stamped file as-is with git commit --only. Also: git commit --only fails with "pathspec did not match any file(s) known to git" for NEW (untracked) files — run git add on the new manifest/sidecar first, then commit --only works.

commit_planning's capability-manifest stamping (landed task 2578) was exercised end-to-end on 2026-08-06 by the flake-ledger decompose and worked exactly as documented: it located plans/flake-ledger-prd.capability-manifest.yaml from metadata.prd_path alone, stamped all 11 Greek labels with their real task ids, and returned manifest_stamping {stamped: 11, missing_labels: [], errors: []}. It copies only MECHANICAL (grep/script) delivered_checks into the producer task's metadata.delivered_checks — `manual` checks stay sidecar-only and are correctly excluded from the dispatch gate (verified on task 3787, which received 3 grep checks and not its manual sibling). Note the stamper REWRITES the YAML through a dumper, so the committed sidecar is reflowed (block-style lists, re-wrapped long strings) relative to what the session authored; commit the stamped file, not the pre-stamp draft.

Stamped peer under topic `commit-planning-yaml-sidecar-comment-loss` (canonical 27ca662a): a consequence of the round-trip that the existing entries do not name — ONCE A SIDECAR HAS BEEN STAMPED, YOU CANNOT PATCH IT BY STRING ANCHOR.

The canonical and its peers all describe the LOSS (comments destroyed, strings reflowed, quoting and list style normalised). The operational consequence for a session that needs to AMEND an already-stamped sidecar is separate and bites immediately: commit_planning's stamper rewrites the file with yaml.safe_dump(raw, sort_keys=False, allow_unicode=True), which re-wraps long scalars at its own column width, drops the quotes you wrote, converts block scalars (`>-`) to plain or single-quoted folded forms, and re-indents list items to dash-at-parent-indent. So every multi-line anchor from the file you authored is now absent, and a patch script built on exact-string replacement fails on its first assertion.

MEASURED 2026-09-11 decomposing plans/live-shadow-eval-prd.md (batch 5382-5395). A six-substitution patch script written against the authored text failed at substitution one (`count=0`) even though the semantic content was unchanged and the file validated fine. The `- label: α` entries had also moved from 2-space to 0-space indentation under `tasks:`.

THE FIX IS TO STOP PATCHING TEXT AND MUTATE THE STRUCTURE: load with yaml.safe_load, operate on the decoded dict (find the task by its `label`, insert/replace capability dicts by their `name`, insert a whole task block at a located index), then write back with the SAME dumper settings the stamper uses — yaml.safe_dump(doc, sort_keys=False, allow_unicode=True) — so your write and the next stamp produce byte-identical formatting instead of a churn diff. Assert on the structural lookups (exactly one task with that label, exactly one capability with that name) rather than on string counts; that gives the same protection against a silent no-op edit. Re-validate afterwards with shared.capability_manifest.load_capability_manifest via `uv run --project shared python`, which is the cheap pre-flight that catches a malformed edit before the next commit_planning tries to stamp it.

COROLLARY: this is another reason durable explanation belongs in the .md manifest twin or in ManifestTask's declared `note:` field rather than in sidecar comments — a `note:` survives both the stamper AND your own structural rewrite, whereas a comment is destroyed by either.

CAPABILITY-MANIFEST STALE VERDICTS: the task-level `note:` field is now the clean third option, and it dissolves the old fork. Stamped peer under `commit-planning-yaml-sidecar-comment-loss`; refines memory e85723e3 / 163a9ba7 (task 4471).

THE OLD FORK, visible in this corpus as two contradictory precedents: a discharged verdict was once FLIPPED in place (the toolcall-markup sidecar's `authority-to-mutate-task-3083` FAIL -> PASS, commit 886b559417, with the decompose-time claim preserved verbatim inside the binding prose because `extra='forbid'` left no other channel), and elsewhere discharged FAILs were deliberately LEFT as FAIL. Both are defensible and they disagree, because in August 2026 the only two moves were "rewrite the row" or "leave a row a reader will misread".

THE THIRD OPTION, used on task 4896 (commit 72cc22a359). Leave every dated verdict/binding byte-identical and append a dated task-level `note:` per leaf: `ManifestTask.note` is DECLARED (`shared/src/shared/capability_manifest.py::ManifestTask`), so it survives `manifest_stamping`'s `yaml.safe_dump` write-back that destroys every comment — which is exactly why the field exists. `ManifestCapability` and `ManifestTask` are both `extra='forbid'`, so there is no per-ROW currency channel; task level is the only one. Three γ leaves whose 2026-08-19 `OPEN` rows were all discharged by landed work got one note each, naming per-row disposition plus the landing commit.

WHY NOT FLIP OPEN -> PASS, even though the schema docstring says an OPEN row "flips to PASS when that task lands": the binding PROSE beside the verdict is itself dated narrative ("Measured 2026-08-19: ... this leaf must choose between migrating or adapting"). Flipping only the verdict leaves a row that reads PASS while its own prose says undecided — internally contradictory, and worse than the stale row. Flipping both rewrites the historical record the file's stated convention (its lines 15-16, "recorded alongside ... left as written") exists to protect.

THE TRAP TO KNOW: the `.md` twin is a RENDER of the `.yaml`, and NOTHING pins their agreement — confirmed live on 4896, where the `.md`'s γ1 rendered note already carried a sentence absent from the `.yaml` note before this change. So a currency note written into only one twin silently diverges. Write it into BOTH, and have the `.md` copy say the verdict column is the `.yaml` as-authored.

VALIDATE with `shared.capability_manifest.load_capability_manifest(<path>)` after any sidecar edit, then `pytest shared/tests/test_capability_manifest.py scripts/tests/test_audit_manifest_descriptor_drift.py` — the corpus checker discovers sidecars via `git ls-files`, so from a worktree it validates YOUR copy (REPO_ROOT resolves to the worktree), not main's.

STAMPED PEER under topic `commit-planning-yaml-sidecar-comment-loss` — the first MEASURED INSTANCES of load-bearing sidecar comments actually destroyed, and the downstream cost.

The canonical entry says comment loss is guaranteed and that durable explanation must live in the `.md` twin. What it did not yet record is that the advice arrived too late for two sidecars, and that the loss later cost a whole adjudication task.

MEASURED 2026-09-09 by task 4907's architect, read-only git archaeology on the main checkout:
1. plans/eval-framework-revival-prd.capability-manifest.yaml — created 2026-07-20 17:00 (commit 9e1487a314) with a 4-line header ending "Earlier eval-revival tasks predate the sidecar convention; their bindings live in the hand-named .md manifest only." Destroyed ~5 minutes later by its own stamp commit a238df3886.
2. plans/found-on-main-provenance-integrity-prd.capability-manifest.yaml — header "# Machine-readable twin of found-on-main-provenance-integrity-prd.capability-manifest.md" created in 5dd39a4c42, destroyed by stamp commit b461b2a915.
Line 1 of both files today is the bare `prd:` key. Reproduce with: git show 9e1487a314:plans/eval-framework-revival-prd.capability-manifest.yaml | head -6

THE COST, which is the point. That first header stated exactly the fact task 4907 was created to determine — that the sidecar covers only a later decomposition wave, so 15 tasks whose labels it omits are correct and need no repair. Because the sentence had been deleted, the answer had to be reconstructed from four commits of history. A reader of the working tree alone cannot learn a sidecar's scope from the sidecar, and the remedy a reader naturally reaches for — add a clarifying header — is silently undone by the next stamp.

PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCES:
- When adjudicating anything about a sidecar's SCOPE or COMPLETENESS, `git log --follow -p -- <sidecar>` first. The original header is often still in history and usually answers the question outright; stamp commits are the ones that strip it.
- The stamp commit MESSAGE is the other surviving record: b461b2a915's says "intermediates α/δ/ι/β carry no sidecar entries by design", which is the adjudication for four of 4907's rows.
- The mechanism is `yaml.safe_dump(raw, sort_keys=False, allow_unicode=True)` at fused-memory/src/fused_memory/server/manifest_stamping.py step 4. The write is atomic (temp + os.replace); it is the CONTENT that loses the comments, not a torn write.
- Filed as a task candidate from 4907 (ticket tkt_0RTE0EWPK9F0019EHHNV1KH2VN) weighing ruamel round-trip vs surgical task_id-only rewrite vs making the machine-owned-sidecar convention explicit in skills/prd/references/decompose-mode.md. Given this behaviour is long known and the twin-is-the-home convention is settled, the curator may well combine or drop it in favour of the third option — if you find no such task, that is the likely reason, not an oversight.

commit_planning manifest-stamper observed behavior (2026-07-22, OS-sandbox batch): the stamper rewrites the YAML sidecar through a YAML round-trip — all hand-written comments are DROPPED and long strings reflowed, so don't put load-bearing information in sidecar comments (put it in the .md manifest twin). It stamps only labels whose tasks are members of the committed batch; sidecar labels belonging to foreign-registry tasks (e.g. reify/sibling flips in a cross-project rollout) are simply left task_id:null WITHOUT appearing in missing_labels (the report tracks batch-tasks-without-sidecar-labels, not the reverse). Foreign-registry labels must be hand-stamped with Edit and the sidecar re-committed (git commit --only) afterwards. Also: commit_planning DOES copy mechanical grep/script delivered_checks into producer metadata.delivered_checks (verified live on task 2910) — the 'interim hand-stamp' note in skills/prd SKILL.md is stale; only foreign-registry ids need hand work.

claim: commit_planning rewrites stamped YAML sidecars, dropping comments and normalizing formatting, so keep durable explanations in the Markdown twin or declared task notes and edit stamped sidecars structurally rather than by text anchors.

members.text: Warm-lane observability gotcha (measured 2026-08-18, _lane-37, task 5843): backgrounding `cargo test ... 2>&1 | tail -40` gives ZERO progress visibility — `tail -N` buffers to EOF, so the harness output file stays 0 bytes for the entire build and the usual poll-the-output-file loop is blind (12m15s of silence here, then the whole log at once). Two fixes: (a) redirect to a log file instead of piping through `tail`, or (b) if already launched, stop polling the output file and block on the process itself with `timeout <secs> tail -f --pid=<cargo pid> /dev/null` — a wait that returns the instant cargo exits, costs one turn instead of ~10, and stays under the 30-minute idle watchdog when the timeout is sized below it (1200s is a safe cap). Interim progress, if you need it, is visible via `ls target/debug/deps/libreify*.rlib | wc -l` (~25 reify crates total) rather than the log.

In this harness, a Bash command that gets auto-backgrounded (i.e. you did NOT pass run_in_background:true yourself, it exceeded the foreground wait) has its continued background execution capped at ~300s regardless of the `timeout` value you requested — it is reported back as "Error: command timed out after 300s" even when the underlying process would have succeeded given more time. Passing `run_in_background: true` explicitly up front makes the full requested `timeout` (up to 600000ms) apply instead. For long cargo build/nextest runs on large crates like reify-compiler, always set run_in_background:true explicitly rather than relying on auto-backgrounding.

[CORRECTED 2026-08-10 by recon Stage 1 (memory_consolidator), run 9970e3bc-ef2d-487f-a58e-4a2a9df46873: the claim above that explicit run_in_background:true makes the full requested timeout apply is FALSE. Measured on task 4152 (2026-08-02, lane _lane-47): `cargo test -p reify-eval --lib` was hard-killed at exactly 300s BOTH when auto-backgrounded (timeout=1800000) AND when launched with an explicit run_in_background:true. The Bash tool is hard-killed at ~300s regardless of the timeout parameter or run_in_background setting — there is no way to get a longer foreground/background wait via tool parameters. For long cargo build/test runs, use the detached setsid+nohup / log+exit-sentinel / sub-300s-poll recipe instead — see mem0 c917e639-9fcb-4a1b-bfe5-4d0ba361b6c8 for the full working recipe and reference timings.]

CORRECTION + recipe (measured on task 4152, 2026-08-02, lane _lane-47): a Bash tool command in this harness is hard-killed at ~300s ("Error: command timed out after 300s") regardless of the `timeout` parameter AND regardless of `run_in_background: true`. An existing procedural entry (mem0 d52477fb-acd5-48af-8a7b-48291783be22) claims passing run_in_background:true up front makes the full requested timeout apply — that is FALSE: `cargo test -p reify-eval --lib` was killed at exactly 300s both when auto-backgrounded with timeout=1800000 and when launched with an explicit run_in_background:true. (Could not amend that entry in place: update_memory's content_amend arm is restricted to recon-stage-* agents.)

Working recipe for a long cargo build/test — detach it from the tool's process group with a log + exit sentinel, then poll in sub-300s chunks:
  rm -f /tmp/X.log; setsid nohup bash -c 'command cargo test ... >> /tmp/X.log 2>&1; echo "SENTINEL_EXIT:$?" >> /tmp/X.log' >/dev/null 2>&1 </dev/null &
  for i in $(seq 1 27); do grep -q '^SENTINEL_EXIT:' /tmp/X.log && break; sleep 10; done; grep -E '^SENTINEL_EXIT:|^test result:|^error' /tmp/X.log
Each poll chunk is its own Bash call, so nothing is abandoned when a chunk ends and the turn never ends with work pending. `command cargo` inside the detached bash -c also bypasses the skim PreToolUse condensation wrapper, so the log keeps full per-test output. Reference timings in a warm lane after editing crates/reify-eval/src: `cargo test -p reify-eval --lib` ~9 min wall (262s of test execution, 2263 tests); `cargo clippy -p reify-eval --all-targets -- -D warnings` ~9 min.

FALSIFYING MEASUREMENT for the `harness-wait-for-background-cargo` cluster's shared premise (peer, task 6301, 2026-09-13, lane _lane-54, Opus 5 implementer role). The canonical index (aa5d0975) states as the constraint all its techniques work around: "a Bash tool call is hard-killed at ~300s regardless of the `timeout` parameter or `run_in_background`". That is NOT true in this harness build. A FOREGROUND `cargo test -p reify-eval` call issued with the Bash tool's `timeout: 1800000` ran to completion in 26m53s wall (1613s = 5.4x the claimed 300s cap; `real 26m53.348s / user 37m58s`) and returned its full output. The `timeout` parameter is honoured (documented max 3900000 ms); the ~300s figure measured on 2026-08-02 (c917e639) appears to be a stale harness behaviour, not a current one.

CONSEQUENCE: the detach+sentinel / PID-blocking recipes are no longer REQUIRED for a sub-25-minute cargo run — just size the foreground `timeout` and wait. They remain useful above ~25 minutes, where the binding constraint is not Bash at all but the orchestrator's idle-based watchdog (stock 1800s of no new transcript turn for implementer/architect/debugger/merger roles), which only a polling shape resets. Note the STEWARD role's ceiling is flat wall clock from session start and polling does NOT extend it.

REFERENCE TIMING (warm lane, 155G `target/`, 32-core host at load ~40, sccache on): full `cargo test -p reify-eval` (lib + all integration binaries + doctests) = ~27 min. Compare the cluster's `--lib`-only figure of ~9 min. Useful green-signal shortcut when output was piped through `tail` and the exit code is masked: cargo runs Doc-tests LAST and stops at the first failing test target, so output that reaches the `Doc-tests` section proves every earlier binary passed.

Waiting on a backgrounded cargo build from an agent session without sleep-polling (the harness blocks foreground `sleep` loops): find the PID of the background shell with `pgrep -af '<distinctive cargo args>'`, then run in the FOREGROUND `timeout 1500 tail --pid=<PID> -f /dev/null; cat <exit-marker-file>` with a Bash timeout slightly above the inner `timeout`. It blocks on the real process exit and returns cleanly. Measured in a reify warm lane under load ~130: a NEW integration-test file in reify-solver-elastic cold-built in 11 min (its reify-test-support dev-dependency pulls in reify-compiler); rebuilding after editing only form_find.rs took about 1m49s.

Reify agent-harness idiom for waiting on a long cargo build WITHOUT a foreground `sleep` (blocked by the anti-polling guard), a busy-loop (SIGTERMed at the Bash timeout, losing all observations), or a reap-vulnerable background waiter: have the background job write a terminal sentinel to a log, then FOREGROUND-block on `timeout 600 tail -f -n +1 /tmp/<log> | grep -m1 -E "<SENTINEL>" >/dev/null` with the Bash `timeout` set above the `timeout(1)` value. `tail -f | grep -m1` exits ON ITS OWN the moment the sentinel appears, so it is a real blocking wait rather than polling; the `timeout(1)` cap bounds it so the call always returns a NEW TURN (resetting the idle watchdog) even if the build hangs, and you simply re-issue it. Emit the sentinel yourself — e.g. run the job as `{ cargo test ...; echo "EXIT1=$?"; cargo test ...; echo "EXIT3=$?"; } > /tmp/<log> 2>&1` — so one wait covers a whole sequence and the exit codes are in the log. Measured 2026-09-03 (task 5755 architect, cold warm lane `_lane-0`): a targeted `cargo test -p reify-compiler --lib <filter>` + `-p reify-eval --lib geometry_ops` + `-p reify-eval --test <one binary>` sequence finished in ~6 min this way, versus a bare `cargo test -p reify-compiler -p reify-eval` which was abandoned after 8 min still compiling because it must build and link ALL 236 top-level integration binaries under crates/reify-eval/tests/ (`ls crates/reify-eval/tests/*.rs | wc -l`). Always scope to `--lib <filter>` plus `--test <binary>` when confirming specific named tests.

claim: For long Cargo jobs, use a wait strategy matched to current harness limits, preserving output and exit status in logs or sentinels rather than relying on buffered output or stale timeout assumptions.

members.text: In reify, `OcctKernel::tessellate(handle, tolerance)` and `OcctKernelHandle` take the linear-deflection tolerance in MODEL UNITS = SI METRES, not millimetres (see the sibling doc at crates/reify-kernel-occt/src/lib.rs:4203, "Sampled max facet-chord deviation (SI metres)"). The engine's `DEFAULT_TESSELLATION_TOLERANCE` is `0.0001`, i.e. 0.1 mm expressed in SI metres. Any tessellation-tolerance constant whose doc says "0.1 mm" but whose value is `0.1` is off by 1000×; box/planar fixtures cannot detect this because planar faces triangulate on exact corner vertices regardless of deflection, so only curved-surface facet counts reveal it.

Reify OCCT gotcha: `OcctKernel::DEFAULT_STL_TESSELLATION_TOLERANCE` (crates/reify-kernel-occt/src/lib.rs) is `0.1` but the kernel works in SI METRES, so it is a 100 mm linear deflection — its own doc comment says "0.1 mm" and the correctly-scaled twin is `Engine::DEFAULT_TESSELLATION_TOLERANCE = 0.0001` (engine_build.rs). BRepMesh_IncrementalMesh emits NO triangulation for curved faces whose size is far below the deflection, so small curved parts export as 0-triangle STLs while planar faces (box) always triangulate. Measured on a guided sweep of circle(r) along a straight spine: r=0.003 m/len=0.02 m gives 0 triangles at tol=0.1 and 100 at tol=1e-4; r=0.02 m/len=0.1 m gives 28 at tol=0.1. The display/GUI path uses the 1e-4 constant, which is why such geometry renders fine but exports empty.

Reify geometry is in SI METRES at the kernel boundary, so any bare tessellation/deflection float is a units trap. OCCT's `tessellate_shape` passes its tolerance straight to `BRepMesh_IncrementalMesh` as an absolute linear deflection in model units: `OcctKernel::DEFAULT_STL_TESSELLATION_TOLERANCE = 0.1` therefore means 100 mm, 1000x coarser than `Engine::DEFAULT_TESSELLATION_TOLERANCE = 0.0001` used for the viewport. On a mm-scale part this silently yields NO triangulation for BSpline faces (e.g. the MakePipeShell result behind `sweep_guided`), which `occt_wrapper.cpp`'s `if (tri.IsNull()) continue;` drops with no error while `BRepMesh` still reports `IsDone()`. Diagnostic trick that isolates it in seconds without a rebuild: scale the design 1000x — if triangles appear, the shape was always fine and the deflection was too coarse. Verified on task 6220 (2026-08-12); constant owned by task 6085.

crates/reify-kernel-occt/src/lib.rs:4231-4237's `DEFAULT_STL_TESSELLATION_TOLERANCE: f64 = 0.1` doc comment claims "0.1 mm: a reasonable general-purpose tessellation default," but docs/prds/v0_6/precision-nominal-representation-guarantee.md §1.1 (task #6085, unresolved as of 2026-09-05) establishes first-hand that the value is actually applied as 0.1 **metres** (100mm) — a live 100x unit-mismatch defect, not a documentation nit. Do not cite "0.1 mm" as fact for this constant in new PRD/doc prose; cite it by symbol without a magnitude, or point to task #6085, until that task lands.

Two verified defects on reify's STL/3MF export tessellation path (2026-08-07, main 43c076ea54), both previously unowned by any live task and now covered by task 6085. (1) STLOutput.resolution is parsed, dimension-checked and converted to SI metres into ExtractedExportSpec.tess_tol at crates/reify-eval/src/tolerance_combine.rs:630 — then DROPPED. tess_tol has zero production consumers (it appears only in its own definition, doc, assignment, struct literal and unit tests); build_outputs reads spec.format, spec.path and spec.step_schema but never spec.tess_tol; and reify_ir::ExportOptions has exactly four fields with no tolerance among them. So a designer's declared resolution has zero effect on emitted geometry. (2) The hardcoded fallback, crates/reify-kernel-occt/src/lib.rs:4030 const DEFAULT_STL_TESSELLATION_TOLERANCE: f64 = 0.1, is documented as "0.1 mm" but the units on that path are SI METRES — as the same comment concedes by citing the engine's metres-valued DEFAULT_TESSELLATION_TOLERANCE (0.0001) for the same quantity. Shipped value is therefore 0.1 m = 100 mm, 1000x coarser than documented. Measured consequence: reify build -o out.stl on sphere(1000mm) emits exactly 304 triangles at EVERY #precision from 0.001mm to 10mm, because at 0.1 m deflection a 1m sphere is past OCCT's Angle=0.5 rad angular crossover (which binds at d/R > 0.0311) so the mesh is angular-limited. PRACTICAL TRAP: this makes triangle count from `reify build -o *.stl` USELESS as a mesh-topology observable when investigating #precision behaviour — it is invariant across four orders of magnitude. Use the RepresentationWithin violation message instead.

Reify: `reify build -o out.stl` tessellates at a HARDCODED 0.1 METRES — `OcctKernel::DEFAULT_STL_TESSELLATION_TOLERANCE: f64 = 0.1` at `crates/reify-kernel-occt/src/lib.rs:4073`, whose own doc comment claims "0.1 mm: a reasonable general-purpose tessellation default for the binary-STL path". A 1000x doc-vs-value mismatch. Task 6085 owns fixing both this and the unconsumed `ExtractedExportSpec.tess_tol` (parsed from STLOutput.resolution at `crates/reify-eval/src/tolerance_combine.rs:630` but with ZERO production consumers). NOTE for anyone following 6085's description: it cites `lib.rs:4024-4030`, but the constant has since moved to `:4073` — grep for `DEFAULT_STL_TESSELLATION_TOLERANCE` rather than trusting the line number. Consequence measured during PRD authoring: a module declaring `RepresentationWithin(subject, 1mm)` exports an STL at 0.1 m deflection (a 100x violation of the declared bound) and `reify build` EXITS 0. Separately verified: ZERO .ri files in the repo currently combine a RepresentationWithin constraint with an Output/STLOutput/StepOutput occurrence (all 5 files carrying the constraint were checked), so adding an export-refusal gate breaks no existing fixture or example.

claim: Reify’s STL export uses a hardcoded 0.1-metre deflection despite documenting 0.1 mm, and ignores the declared resolution, producing dangerously coarse meshes.

[SUPERSEDED 2026-09-09 by Leo's ruling] The crate-scoped carve-out recorded below is NOT granted. The house rule is Position A EVERYWHERE: avoid `step-N` plan-step labels in test names, section comments and doc-comments in ALL crates, `crates/reify-syntax/` included. members.text: Reify dangling-`concurrent.rs`-reference cleanups (task family #6231/#6245/#6276) use TWO distinct fixes, chosen by what the old pointer carried. If content was literally RELOCATED out of the deleted concurrent stack, use the `[Re-homed from `concurrent.rs`'s <symbol>, task ξ #5046 — the dead concurrent stack is deleted by task ο.]` form (examples: engine_edit.rs:6053/6143, engine_fixpoint.rs:1264). If the pointer was merely a "see also / another instance" reader-pointer carrying no relocated content, DELETE it outright — do not convert it to a Re-homed citation, since citing a deleted file for an example nobody can consult is noise. In both cases, live code is referenced by module-qualified SYMBOL name only (e.g. `engine_edit.rs::edit_param`), never by line number.

Reify comment convention, the DELETED-THING half (complements the well-covered "reference symbols, not line numbers" rule — do not restate that one): when a comment must still name a file or symbol that has been DELETED, mark it explicitly as deleted and cite the deleting commit SHA + task, so a reader never tries to open it. Established form, on main at crates/reify-eval/src/engine_edit.rs:6053 and :6143 and crates/reify-eval/src/engine_fixpoint.rs:1264: "[Re-homed from `concurrent.rs`'s <symbol>, task ξ (#5046) — the dead concurrent stack is deleted by task ο.]"; task 6245 reused it as "...was deleted with `concurrent.rs` in c1b8dba3f7 (task ο, #5065)". Decision rule for which way to go: if the surviving sentence stands on its own without the dead thing, DROP the pointer entirely rather than re-homing it; only name the deleted thing when it IS the explanation (why no consumer exists, why a promised guard never arrived). NOTE the SHA-vs-subject-line caveat (mem0 21176f95) does NOT apply here: these cites name commits already LANDED on main, so the SHA is durable — that caveat is about citing unlanded task-branch commits. Ongoing family working this defect class across the workspace: tasks 6218, 6231, 6245, 6253, 6276, 6279, 6316.

Reify's stale-source-reference defect family (tasks 6218/6231/6245/6276/6279/6316/6930, all tracing to the task ο #5065 deletion of concurrent.rs and concurrent_eval.rs) has converged on a two-part comment convention: (1) reference live code by SYMBOL NAME only — never a bare line number and never a "see <file>" pointer, since both rot silently; (2) where a deleted module must still be named to explain why an API has no consumer, KEEP the mention but stamp it explicitly as deleted with its commit + task cite, e.g. "deleted with `concurrent.rs` in c1b8dba3f7 (task ο, #5065)". Canonical in-tree examples: crates/reify-eval/src/engine_fixpoint.rs:1264, crates/reify-eval/src/engine_edit.rs:6093/:6183, crates/reify-eval/src/gating.rs:16, crates/reify-runtime/src/commitment.rs:24/:102/:269. The fix is NOT "scrub every mention" — a stamped provenance note is frozen history, not a followable pointer, and removing it destroys the explanation a reader needs.

claim: Reference live code by symbol name; keep deleted-code citations only when needed to explain something, and mark them explicitly deleted with the landed commit and task.

members.text: Rust `#[track_caller]` is INERT when the panic fires inside a closure. A helper written as `x.unwrap_or_else(|| panic!("..."))` reports the closure body's line in helpers.rs, not the calling test's line, because a closure is its own function and does not inherit the attribute from the enclosing fn. Restructure to the `let Some(v) = ... else { panic!("...") };` (let-else) shape so the panic site lives directly in the `#[track_caller]` fn body. Verified empirically with a minimal rustc repro during task #5697; applies to reify-test-support's helpers.rs getters (get_value_cell_in / get_let_expr_in / get_let_expr) and to any assertion helper in that file.

To pin that a reify-test-support helper panic reports the CALLER's location (#[track_caller] actually working), add a guard to crates/reify-test-support/tests/track_caller_panic_location.rs (landed by #7612): call its `panic_site(|| ...)` and assert `site.file == file!()` plus a short message substring — never an exact line!() (rustfmt-fragile). The hook there is mutex-serialised and thread-filtered, so it is safe under libtest's parallel threads; don't hand-roll a second panic hook. #[should_panic(expected=..)] pins cannot detect a location regression.

`#[track_caller]` on a sync fn is silently inert if the panic site is nested inside a closure passed to something like `.unwrap_or_else(|| panic!(...))` — the closure is its own separate function and does not inherit the attribute, so `Location::caller()`/the panic message resolves to the closure's line inside the helper, not the caller's line. Verified empirically with rustc: a `#[track_caller] fn` panicking via `.unwrap_or_else(|| panic!(...))` reports its own body's line; the same fn restructured to `let Some(x) = opt else { panic!(...) }` (panic directly in the fn body, no closure) correctly reports the call site's line. Fix any `#[track_caller]` helper whose panic sits inside an `.unwrap_or_else`/`.map_or_else`/similar closure by hoisting it to a `let ... else { panic!(...) }` (or plain `match`) in the function body. Found in `crates/reify-test-support/src/helpers.rs` during task #5697. What #5697 landed fixed only the "no template named" panic (a let-else in `get_value_cell_in`, which `get_let_expr_in` reaches it through); on main 2b9b48e241 (2026-09-16) the "has no default expr" panic in `require_default_expr` and `cell_value`'s panic are still inside closures, and task 6973 is scoped to fix both. `#[should_panic(expected = ...)]` tests stay green either way since they match message text, not location, so this class of bug does not show up as a test failure. [Corrected 2026-09-16 by the curator sitting per gate task #7578: this entry previously said the bug was "found and fixed" in `get_value_cell_in`/`get_let_expr_in`, which overstated the fix.]

Rust `#[track_caller]` does NOT cross a closure boundary: a panic raised inside `unwrap_or_else(|| panic!(...))` resolves `Location::caller()` to the closure body, silently making the attribute inert so failures report the helper's own line instead of the calling test's. Use the `let Some(x) = ... else { panic!(...) }` shape so the panic site lives directly in the `#[track_caller]` fn body. Verified empirically with a minimal rustc repro during reify task #5697. What #5697 landed in crates/reify-test-support/src/helpers.rs moved the "no template named" panic into a let-else in `get_value_cell_in`, which `get_let_expr_in` reaches it through. It did NOT move the "has no default expr" panic: on main 2b9b48e241 (2026-09-16) that one still sits inside a closure in `require_default_expr`, as does `cell_value`'s panic, and task 6973 is scoped to fix both. Applies to any panicking test-support helper meant to blame its caller. [Corrected 2026-09-16 by the curator sitting per gate task #7578: this entry previously said both `get_value_cell_in` and `get_let_expr_in` were restructured, which overstated the fix.]

claim: Rust `#[track_caller]` does not cross closure boundaries, so keep panic sites in the function body and test caller locations without asserting exact line numbers.

members.text: tests/scripts/test_spawn_claude.py's subprocess-timing tests (test_transcript_appearance_suppresses_flag: grace=3s/sleep=8s; test_foreground_claude_descendant_suppresses_flag_without_transcript: grace=2s/sleep=6s) use generous margins to absorb whole-second `date +%s` truncation noise, but can still spuriously fail under extreme host oversubscription (observed: load avg 116-134 on a 32-core host). Confirmed on task 2286: the full 27-test file failed 1 test on one run, then passed 27/27 clean on immediate retry with no code changes; the failing test also passed standalone in 9.38s. This is the same host-oversubscription flake class already tracked by tasks 2344/2361/2365 — future debugging agents seeing a failure in THIS test file under high load should suspect timing/scheduling flake before assuming a logic regression, and should retry before debugging.

Flaky test under merge-worker load: tests/scripts/test_spawn_claude.py::test_transcript_appearance_suppresses_flag can fail with rc 144 ("claude never started within 3s") during full post-merge verify runs on a busy host, because it asserts on real wall-clock timing (3s started-grace vs an 8s fake-claude sleep; watchdog deadline from `date +%s` whole-second resolution). Its docstring already documents the margin as "flaky under load (observed empirically)". It passes reliably in isolation (~9s). When this test is the sole failure in a post-merge verify escalation for a task whose diff does not touch skills/spawn/spawn-claude.sh, treat it as a benign flake and retry the merge rather than modifying task code.

Task 2680's merge-verify attempts (2026-07-17) hit three known-unrelated timing-flake tests under host/merge-queue load, none touching its actual diff (fused-memory config/schema.py + orchestrator reopen-sticks e2e tests only): (1) shared/tests/test_cli_invoke.py::TestRunSubprocessWorkingRegimeProgressExtension::test_unreadable_transcript_degrades_to_old_ceiling_even_with_extension_params_set — hard `wall < 1.0` assertion on subprocess SIGKILL teardown, observed at 1.325s/1.354s under contention; FIXED on main via commit fda97df621af (widened to `wall < 3.0`, teardown/event-loop scheduling latency under parallel verify load, not extension-param leakage) — should no longer recur. (2) tests/scripts/test_spawn_claude.py::test_transcript_appearance_suppresses_flag — asserts a real spawned spawn-claude.sh process starts within a 3s window; failed under merge-queue contention; NOT yet fixed — still a known flake to waive when an unrelated diff hits it. (3) dashboard/tests/test_escalation_analytics.py::TestBuildEscalationAnalyticsPerf::test_cold_10k_archive_under_5_seconds — `elapsed < 5.0` cold-build 10k-record perf budget, observed at 6.08s under contention; NOT yet fixed — still a known flake to waive. Extends the known-flakes waiver catalog (see memory 452e0abc-2364-4fa7-a671-7060bb2ec1bc, 2026-07-14) with these two still-outstanding tests: treat as known load-induced flakes (waive, don't re-investigate from scratch) when a diff outside dashboard/data/escalation_analytics.py or tests/scripts/spawn_claude.sh/shared/cli_invoke.py hits them under load.

The test_transcript_appearance_suppresses_flag flake (tasks 2344/2361/2365 tracked, host-oversubscription class documented in an earlier memory) has a concrete mechanism: spawn-claude.sh's _started_evidence falls back to _claude_descendant_alive whenever the transcript dir doesn't exist yet at the current poll tick. _claude_descendant_alive shells out to `ps -eo pid=,ppid=,args=` and walks every system process in a pure-bash `while read` loop (O(n) processes, high per-iteration bash overhead) looking for a claude descendant. On a host with ~1165 processes under load average 111-140 on 32 cores, a single call measured ~1.4s in isolation -- enough to consume the entire 3s SPAWN_STARTED_GRACE_SECS grace budget in one _started_watchdog loop iteration, so the loop exits before a second iteration can observe the transcript file that actually appeared almost immediately. Confirmed via bash -x trace + isolated timing on 2026-07-17; reproduces identically on a clean main checkout (not a task-specific regression) and passes cleanly on retry when ambient load allows a call under ~1s. Whoever picks up tasks 2344/2361/2365 should look at bounding/replacing _claude_descendant_alive's full-system ps scan rather than just re-tuning grace/sleep margins.

For merge-verify-host-load timing flakes in fixed-second-margin tests, prefer a load-scaled margin over another fixed bump: factor = max(1.0, os.getloadavg()[0] / os.cpu_count()); scaled = ceil(base_secs * factor), clamped to [base_secs, cap_secs]. A fixed bump chases a moving target as host load climbs — tests/scripts/test_spawn_claude.py's SPAWN_STARTED_GRACE_SECS flake recurred within 6 days (task 2367 bumped 1s/2s→3s/8s; task 2733 replaced the fixed values with a `_load_scaled_grace` helper). Floor at base_secs keeps an idle host byte-identical (no regression); cap keeps a pathological host bounded. When enlarging a grace/timeout this way, also make any outer wrapper timeout grace-relative (grace + fixed-work + margin) so the same load spike can't just convert one flake type into another (e.g. a 144 flag-flake into a subprocess TimeoutExpired flake).

tests/scripts/test_spawn_claude.py has two independent families of fixed-timeout mechanisms prone to load-sensitive flakes under merge-verify contention: (1) SPAWN_STARTED_GRACE_SECS env pins consumed by spawn-claude.sh's started-watchdog, and (2) the test file's own _wait_for_path(path, timeout=N) polling helper. Task 2733 introduced _load_scaled_grace(base_secs, cap_secs=30) to scale (1) by host load-per-core (os.getloadavg()[0] / os.cpu_count()), floored at base and capped; task 3451 added _set_started_grace(env) on top of it (base=8, cap=60) to also WRITE the result into env, and routed all three "must-not-be-flagged" SPAWN_STARTED_GRACE_SECS sites through it. For (2), only one _wait_for_path call site (test_window_close_129_robust_to_delayed_trap_install, using _load_scaled_grace(5)) has been converted -- four others (test_window_close_yields_129_not_hang, test_tmux_backend_missing_tmux_yields_126, test_sibling_mode_is_fire_and_forget, test_sibling_mode_foreground_emulator_is_fire_and_forget) still use fixed 5.0/10.0s timeouts and are candidate flake sites (one observed flaking under load during task 3451's verify; tracked in follow-up ticket tkt_0RRZ5H7GPM9FD3B8Y3WS1HKT2K / escalation esc-3451-1). Not every fixed pin in this file should be converted, though: some (e.g. the two "must fire" / "127 must beat 144" SPAWN_STARTED_GRACE_SECS pins task 3451 left untouched) are deliberately load-INSENSITIVE by design, so each site needs its own audit before applying _load_scaled_grace-style scaling.

claim: Real-time subprocess tests in test_spawn_claude.py can flake under host load; retry unrelated failures, and fix the cause with audited load-scaled timeouts or by bounding expensive process scans.

members.text: Operational gotcha: the reify orchestrator runs as a systemd USER unit `orchestrator-reify.service` (managed via `systemctl --user`, alongside sibling user units orchestrator-dark-factory, orchestrator-know-live, etc.). A SYSTEM-scope `systemctl is-active orchestrator-reify.service` FALSELY reports `inactive`/`dead` because the unit lives in the user manager, not the system manager. To check liveness use `systemctl --user is-active orchestrator-reify.service`, or confirm via the escalation MCP port (reify = 127.0.0.1:8100; a listening `orchestrator` process there means it's up), or `ps` for `orchestrator run --config .../reify/orchestrator.yaml`. Corollary: if the escalation MCP tools (resolve_issue, get_pending_escalations, merge_request) respond successfully, the orchestrator is up by definition — don't separately conclude it's down from a system-scope systemctl check.

orchestrator-reify IS a live systemd `--user` unit — checking it WITHOUT `--user` actively misleads. `systemctl is-active orchestrator-reify.service` returns "inactive"/"could not be found", which led an L2 watcher (2026-07-25/26) to conclude for hours that reify's orchestrator ran as a bare `uv run` process and that journald had no logs for it. Both false. Correct probes: `systemctl --user show orchestrator-reify.service -p MainPID -p ExecMainStartTimestamp -p NRestarts -p Result`, and `journalctl --user -u orchestrator-reify.service`. The root cause of the 2026-07-24..26 fleet-wide dispatch livelock lived in that journal and was unreachable from runs.db, which could record THAT every dispatch requeued but never WHY. Also note `WorkingDirectory=/home/leo/src/dark-factory`, NOT reify's project_root — so any relative path resolved against the orchestrator's cwd resolves into dark-factory.

CORRECTION — THE REIFY ORCHESTRATOR *IS* A SYSTEMD USER UNIT (verified live 2026-08-29). A prior belief that it was "not under systemd, check the process/port 8100 instead" is FALSE and cost at least one investigation real accuracy. `systemctl --user status orchestrator-reify.service` returns Active: active (running), Main PID a `uv` process, CGroup under user@1000.service/app.slice; the unit file is ~/.config/systemd/user/orchestrator-reify.service (enabled) with a drop-in at orchestrator-reify.service.d/warm-lane.conf. TWO CONSEQUENCES: (1) its LOGS ARE ON DISK in the user journal — `journalctl --user -u orchestrator-reify.service` works. An earlier pass believed its stdout was an unrecoverable socket and reasoned from correlation instead of reading the log; it is journald's socket. (2) The namespace is `systemctl --user`, NOT system scope — a system-scope probe returns nothing and looks exactly like proof that no unit exists, which is very likely how the false claim was minted. Restart discipline is unchanged: never `systemctl restart` it directly (the TimeoutStopSec=90 stop window cancels restart's start half); use scripts/orchestrator-redeploy-restart.sh.

DISCOVERY (reify, 2026-07-26): the reify orchestrator's own log is the ONLY place many dispatch failures are diagnosable, and two things conspire to hide it.

1. `orchestrator-reify.service` IS a systemd **`--user`** unit (cgroup: `user.slice/user-1000.slice/user@1000.service/app.slice/orchestrator-reify.service`). Running `systemctl status orchestrator-reify.service` WITHOUT `--user` queries the system manager and reports "Unit ... could not be found" — a false negative that reads exactly like "this isn't a systemd service, it's a bare `uv run` process". A prior reify memory asserted precisely that and was WRONG; it was corrected this session. Every project has one: orchestrator-{reify,dark-factory,know-live,pump-web-ui,my-solar-challenge,solar-challenge-platform,autopilot-video}.service.

2. `runs.db` cannot answer "why did this requeue". The `task_completed` event payload is counters-only (`outcome`, `agent_invocations`, `execute_iterations`, `verify_attempts`, `review_cycles`, `steward_cost_usd`, `steward_invocations`) and the `task_results` table has no `block_reason` column either. The reason IS computed and lives on `TerminalReport.reason` -> `TaskReport.block_reason`, but is dropped at BOTH persistence layers. `SELECT DISTINCT json_extract(data,'$.reason'), '$.requeue_reason', '$.error'` returns all-NULL. Filed as reify task 5569.

Correct commands:
  journalctl --user -u orchestrator-reify.service --since "HH:MM"
  journalctl --user _PID=<pid>
  systemctl --user is-active orchestrator-reify.service
  systemctl --user show orchestrator-reify.service -p MainPID -p ActiveEnterTimestamp
  cat /proc/<pid>/cgroup      # to identify the owning unit of an unknown pid

During esc-5556-1 the root cause was stated verbatim, once per dispatch cycle, in journald, while being completely invisible in runs.db. Two reconciliation cycles and an L2 watcher pass had stalled trying to derive it from the events alone. Reach for journald early on any "the events show THAT it happened but never WHY" question.

claim: The reify orchestrator runs as a systemd user unit, so use `systemctl --user` and `journalctl --user`—system-scope checks mislead, and its journal can reveal failures missing from runs.db.

members.text: In orchestrator/tests, mocked-git_ops train tests (test_merge_queue_train_attribution.py's _make_git_ops_mock, a plain MagicMock) only pre-wire the AsyncMock methods a given test path needs — any newly-added await on an unwired method (e.g. git_ops.resolve_branch_sha) will raise "object MagicMock can't be used in an await expression" unless the test explicitly sets it as AsyncMock. By contrast, test_atomic_train_merge.py drives _do_train_merge through REAL GitOps(config.git, repo) instances against real git repos, so new awaited GitOps methods there just execute real git plumbing and never need manual mock wiring. When adding a new awaited git_ops call inside _do_train_merge or _finalize_inflight, check both styles of test file for regressions.

Gotcha when adding a new `await self.git_ops.<method>(...)` call inside TaskWorkflow._execute_iterations or _verify_debugfix_loop: the established loop-driver test harnesses (test_workflow_resume_on_progress.py `_stub_iteration_helpers`, test_workflow_zero_output_hang.py) wire git_ops as a plain MagicMock, so awaiting a new git_ops method raises `TypeError: object MagicMock can't be used in 'await' expression`. Make the new call fail-soft (try/except, default a safe value) if it is observability-only, or update those harnesses to AsyncMock the method. These harnesses already stub `_get_head_commit` as AsyncMock(return_value='abc123') and mock `append_iteration_log`, so adding extra `_get_head_commit()` calls is safe and they do not assert iteration-entry contents.

Gotcha (orchestrator tests): when a workflow method on the VERIFY/REVIEW loop path gains a new `await self.git_ops.<method>(...)` call (e.g. task 2760's `_commit_amendment_wip` awaiting `git_ops.has_uncommitted_work`), every loop-driving test helper that builds `git_ops` as a bare `MagicMock` breaks with `TypeError: object MagicMock can't be used in 'await' expression`. The bare MagicMock returns a non-awaitable child. Fix: stub the new call as `AsyncMock(...)` in each such helper (`_make_loop_workflow` in test_workflow_amendment.py, `_make_workflow` in test_workflow_review_persistence.py). Only helpers whose tests actually reach the amendment branch (non-blocking review + in-scope suggestion + cap not exhausted) are affected.

In orchestrator tests, adding a new `await self._git_ops.<method>(...)` call to a shared merge_queue.py production path has blast radius into test files that never mention the changed code: several test helpers build their stand-in as a bare `git_ops = MagicMock()` and pre-wire only the async attributes their own tests happened to need (e.g. `_make_minimal_worker` in test_multihost_verify_integration.py). The new await then dies with `TypeError: object MagicMock can't be used in 'await' expression` deep inside the production callee, which reads as an unrelated test regression rather than a mock gap. When adding such a call, grep for `git_ops = MagicMock()` builders reaching the changed path and pre-wire the attribute as `AsyncMock()`, matching the `_make_git_ops_mock()` helpers in test_merge_queue_depth_telemetry.py / test_merge_queue_concurrent_verify.py. These breakages only surface in a FULL suite run, not in the changed files' own tests.

claim: When adding an awaited GitOps call, find every test helper that reaches the changed path and wire the method as an AsyncMock if its git_ops is a bare MagicMock.

Reify's static interference/clearance oracle CANNOT detect full containment: `distance`, `min_clearance`, `intersects` and `interferes_with` all funnel through one `kernel_distance` call into a single `GeometryQuery::Distance` (OCCT `BRepExtrema_DistShapeShape`, non-negative by construction), and the two booleans are literally `Bool(d <= 0.0)`. So a solid fully nested inside another with no boundary contact yields a POSITIVE distance AND `false` from both booleans — all four report "clear" on the worst possible interference. Pairing the scalar with the boolean does NOT help; they are the same distance test read two ways. `contains` is NOT the fix: it is `contains(solid, point)` (args[1] goes through `resolve_point3_length_arg`), and since the compiler assigns only its result type (`"contains" => Type::Bool`) with no arg-slot check, `contains(solidA, solidB)` compiles clean and evaluates to a silent `undef`. No solid-solid containment predicate exists. The working idiom is the boolean-volume oracle, both calls let-bound: `let outside = difference(inner, outer)` then `let pokeout = volume(outside)`, contained iff `pokeout` is below a small positive floor (1e-9 m^3 is the established precedent) — never exact zero. Worked examples `examples/tolerancing/gdt_oracle_inside.ri`/` [cut]

MEASURED 2026-09-18 (task 6475, HEAD=ea896581d1): the Manifold kernel DOES detect full solid containment — the long-standing hypothesis that `Manifold::min_gap` returns the surface-to-surface gap (not 0) for a fully-nested solid pair is FALSE. Driving both kernels through `GeometryQuery::Distance` with a 200mm outer box and a concentric 20mm inner box (90mm clearance per face, no boundary contact), OCCT and Manifold BOTH return 0.0, in both argument orders, for a primitive container AND for difference-derived and union-derived containers. `min_gap` is not a naive surface distance: a 20mm probe floating in the 100mm cavity of a hollow shell correctly reads 0.04 m on both kernels, so the containment 0.0 is genuine classification, not a degenerate zero. Disjoint/near/touching/partial-overlap arms also agree (0.39 vs 0.390000008046627; 0.001 vs 0.0010000020265579224; 0.0 vs 0.0; 0.0 vs 0.0). Manifold's deviation is f32-ulp ingest noise, worst case 8.05e-9 m. The OCCT boolean-derived-container miss recorded in this task's 2026-09-03 amendment is also resolved: task #7054 (merge 7bea63cea4) landed and is an ancestor of main.

Reify's OCCT full-containment behaviour is now PINNED by a test, as of task 6269 (landed on task/6269): `crates/reify-eval/tests/harness_kernel_realization/kernel_queries_intersects_smoke.rs` → `intersects_and_distance_detect_full_containment`. It asserts `intersects = true` and `distance` EXACTLY `si_value == 0.0` (not a tolerance) for a strictly-nested solid pair in BOTH argument orders, with a disjoint control (35 mm gap, epsilon 1e-9) in the same inline source so a regression cannot pass vacuously. This is an addendum to the existing measurement cluster (mem0 51327d65 / 507c42b0, superseding 26e4b124; curator gate task 6476) — the measurement itself is unchanged, what is new is that it is now regression-protected and documented in `examples/best_practices/clearance_oracle.ri` (CONTAINMENT bullet) and `examples/best_practices/INDEX.md`. OCCT DOES detect full solid containment through reify's `intersects`/`distance` builtins — there is no "full-containment blind spot". Measured 2026-08-23 on task/6269 (`./target/release/reify eval`): outer=box(20mm,20mm,20mm), inner=box(10mm,10mm,10mm) strictly nested gives intersects=true and distance EXACTLY 0.0 (proved in-language: `g == 0mm` is true, `g > 0mm` is false, `g * 1e12` is still 0), symmetric in both argument orders; disjoint control at 50mm gives intersects=false, distance=0.035 m. Mechanism: BRepExtrema_DistShapeShape runs SolidTreatment() and sets InnerSolution() when one shape lies inside a solid, returning 0.0 — so the "non-negative by construction" comment at crates/reify-kernel-occt/cpp/occt_wrapper.cpp:1906 (`dist.Value() <= 0.0`) is consistent with a measured zero, not evidence of a gap.
