members.text: jcodemunch-mcp 1.108.54 emits 3-segment MUNCH `__tables` specs (`prefix:table:cols`, e.g. `r:__rows__:file|specifier|match_type`) with the trailing type list OMITTED, and its `find_references` rows carry no `line` column at all. In reify-audit's `jcodemunch_client.rs`, a type-less spec decodes EVERY column as `ColType::Str`, so any wire adapter reading a numeric column with a bare `?.as_u64()` / `?.as_f64()` inside its `filter_map` silently drops the whole row — turning a grammar drift into a silently-empty `Vec` (an audit reporting a clean corpus) instead of a loud `LoadError::Protocol`. Read mandatory numeric columns through `row_u64` / `row_f64` (number-or-string-parse), and treat `line == 0` as the documented "wire did not report one" sentinel rather than a drop condition.

jcodemunch's MUNCH/1 `__tables=` spec has TWO grammars that differ by serve version: 1.108.27 (the captured fixtures in crates/reify-audit/tests/fixtures/jcodemunch/) emits 4 colon-segments `<prefix>:<table>:<cols>:<types>`, while 1.108.54 emits 3 for find_references — `r:__rows__:file|specifier|match_type`, i.e. the type list omitted (treat all columns as str). A MUNCH decoder must accept both. Separately, jcodemunch's find_references returns IMPORT-site records shaped {file, specifier, match_type} with NO line number, and the files it names are importers — never the declaring file (measured 2026-08-24: JCodemunchOps -> 4 refs, none of them the lib.rs that declares it).

reify-audit's captured jcodemunch wire fixtures under crates/reify-audit/tests/fixtures/jcodemunch/ are jcodemunch-mcp 1.108.27-era and do NOT reflect the pinned 1.108.54 serve: 1.108.54 emits 3-segment MUNCH `__tables` specs (e.g. `r:__rows__:file|specifier|match_type`, per-column type list omitted) where the fixtures are all 4-segment. A green fixture suite is therefore NOT evidence the client decodes the live wire — that gap made every find_references call fail to decode for months (task #6447). A 3-segment spec also decodes every column as ColType::Str, so numeric columns like `line` arrive as JSON strings and a bare `.as_u64()?` inside a filter_map adapter silently drops the whole row.

claim: MUNCH clients must handle version-dependent three- and four-segment specs, parse numeric strings, and tolerate missing find_references line numbers to avoid silently dropping rows.

members.text: A user module's `CompiledModule.trait_defs` holds ONLY the traits that module itself declares — `structure def X : Rigid` compiles to a module with an EMPTY `trait_defs`, because `Rigid` and its `Rigid : Physical` refinement edge live in the stdlib prelude (crates/reify-compiler/stdlib/structural_physical.ri). So any `reify_eval::tolerance_combine::conforms_to_trait` / `conforms_to_output` conformance check must be resolved against the MERGED module + `Engine::prelude()` trait defs (helper `merged_trait_defs` in gui/src-tauri/src/engine.rs; mirrored by `engine_build.rs::build_outputs_with_result`). Passing the bare module set compiles fine and silently degrades the check to direct-bound-name matching with no test failure — that is the class of bug tracked as #5558 in `build_template_node`'s `trait_geometry` gate. CORRECTION (2026-09-16, reconciliation run 97cb15c1): this note's original "fixed" framing described only branch `task/5558`'s then-current state (refinement-chain fix test-green there since 2026-07-28, polished further 2026-09-15 ~22:38-22:42 UTC, 988 tests passing). As of 2026-09-15 that fix has NOT merged to `main` — `main` still uses the literal `.contains("Physical")` substring check at gui/src-tauri/src/engine.rs (confirmed by direct git inspection). Do not treat #5558 as shipped/fixed in the mainline codebase until the branch merges. UPDATE (2026-09-16, reconciliation run 65bd8a6f, memory_consolidator): task 5558's status has since progressed — get_task(5558) now shows status='in-progress' (updatedAt 2026-09-16T07:10:46Z) with a `merge_retry_pending` entry (branch_head fa92746e, base_sha 43a442d8) indicating the branch attempted a merge to main that has not yet landed. Task 5558 is therefore no longer `pending`; its current state is `in-progress (branch attempted merge, not yet landed)`. The core factual claim above — that main still uses the literal `.contains("Physical")` substring check until that merge lands — is unaffected.

In reify-compiler, a `trait` body compiled standalone (no conforming structure) emits NO dimension diagnostics: `constraint material.density > 1m` (Density vs Length), `let bad = mass + 1m` on a plain identifier, and even a reference to a wholly undefined member field all produce zero error diagnostics. The identical expressions inside a `structure` DO produce `DimensionMismatch`. Consequence: any test asserting the ABSENCE of a diagnostic (e.g. `assert_no_error_diagnostics` in polymorphic_zero_tests.rs) is VACUOUS if written against a bare trait body — it passes regardless of the behaviour under test. Write such probes as a `structure`, and pair them with a non-vacuity guard asserting that a deliberately-mismatched NON-ZERO literal still errors. Measured task 6038 at HEAD 5370e7a13f; see `member_access_mismatched_non_zero_still_errors` in crates/reify-compiler/tests/polymorphic_zero_tests.rs.

[CORRECTION 2026-09-14 (post-6038 re-check): the cited worked-example path was wrong even at landing — task 6038 pivoted mid-development (commit 0555b551d3) to host the 3 eval pins inside the harness_engine integration-test binary. Correct path: crates/reify-eval/tests/harness_engine/polymorphic_zero_trait_eval.rs. The '3 pins' count itself is accurate (trait_body_member_access_gt_bare_zero_satisfied, trait_body_inherited_param_gt_bare_zero_satisfied, trait_body_member_access_gt_bare_zero_violated_when_zero).]

Reify testing technique — how to pin a constraint that GENUINELY must live in a trait body. The known gotcha (memories 06e35691, eea5b075, 10c6eb04) says a bare trait body is not dimension-checked, so rewrite the probe as a `structure`. That works for breadth pins, but not when the stdlib site under test IS a trait and the trait-ness is the point (structural_physical.ri `trait Physical { constraint material.density > 0kg/m^3 }`, materials_electrical.ri `trait Insulating { constraint dielectric_strength > 0.0V/m }`). For those, drop to EVAL level: `reify_test_support::check_source_with_stdlib` (needs reify-eval's existing `eval-helpers` dev-dep feature; no Cargo.toml change), declare the trait plus a conforming structure, and assert `reify_ir::Satisfaction::Satisfied` on every injected constraint result — plus a non-empty check so a conformer that injected nothing cannot pass vacuously, and a paired `Violated` case on a value that genuinely fails the bound. Assert the Satisfaction VALUE, never "no error": a regressed dimension coercion makes `eval_cmp` compare Scalar-vs-Real and degrade SILENTLY to `Indeterminate` + a ConstraintIndeterminate warning rather than erroring, so only an equality assertion converts that into a test failure. Worked example: crates/reify-eval/tests/polymorphic_zero_trait_eval.rs (task 6038, 3 pins).

Reify trait-body checking is DEFERRED to conformance: a `trait` compiled with NO conforming structure emits ZERO error diagnostics no matter how broken its body is — dimension-mismatched constraints, references to undefined member fields, and wrong `let` type annotations all pass silently. Adding a conformer (`structure def C : T { ... }`) makes all three fire (`DimensionMismatch`, `StructureMemberNotFound`, `TypeMismatchForTraitMember` respectively). Consequence: an absence-of-diagnostic assertion (`assert_no_error_diagnostics` / `assert_no_diagnostics`) written against a bare trait body is VACUOUS — it passes regardless of what the compiler does. The vacuity condition is precisely "trait body with no conformer", NOT "trait body". Measured on main @ 6927f3c0db (task 6143); pinned in crates/reify-compiler/tests/harness_traits/trait_body_deferred_check_tests.rs.

claim: Trait behavior is context-dependent: resolve conformance with prelude traits and test constraints through conformers with explicit outcomes, since bare trait compilation can silently skip checks.

SIGHTING + NUANCE under topic `guard-tests-grep-code-not-prose` (task 3226, review cycle 2, blocking): the prose-vs-code rule bites even when a guard scans its OWN module's source, not another file's. `tests/scripts/test_check_lock_charter_drift.py::test_module_import_resolves_no_checkout_at_module_scope` did `src = Path(drift.__file__).read_text()` and failed on any column-0 line containing `resolve_reify_checkout(`. Because `src.splitlines()` includes the module docstring and that docstring's lines ARE at column 0, and because the module's prose necessarily EXPLAINS the very construct being banned, rewording the docstring — changing zero code — turned it red. Self-ownership does not rescue a text scan; if anything it guarantees the false positive, since the rationale and the banned token are the same string.

THE EXECUTABLE DISCRIMINATOR (use this to classify any suspected prose-pin, and to confirm a fix): insert a column-0 line naming the banned construct INTO the module docstring, change no code, and run the guard. Red => it is a prose/comment-content pin. Green => it is referential integrity. This is a two-line diff and settles the question without argument.

AST FORM PASSES THE DISCRIMINATOR — measured, not assumed. Two sibling guards in the same file (`test_source_contains_no_parents_index_arithmetic`, `test_no_ambient_environ_reread`) route through an `ast.parse()` helper instead of `read_text()`. Injecting column-0 docstring prose naming `Path(__file__).parents[5]` and `os.environ` left both GREEN (2 passed). A resume briefing had asserted these two carried the same defect; running the discriminator showed they do not. So: when a structural guard must ban a construct the module's own docs discuss, `ast.parse` + `ast.walk` is the fix, and it is also strictly stronger (it catches `x.parents [3]` and an aliased `par = p.parents; par[3]`).

DELETION IS OFTEN THE RIGHT FIX, BUT VERIFY THE CLAIMED REPLACEMENT COVERAGE FIRST. The 3226 review justified deleting the scan by claiming a sibling subprocess-import assertion already covered the invariant. Tested: it does NOT — a genuine module-scope `resolve_reify_checkout(...)` call leaves that subprocess import PASSING, because the function returns rather than raising. The real cover was elsewhere (`TestResolve`'s cases set the env var AFTER import, so they detect the actual harm — an un-steerable import-frozen answer; freezing the answer in a module-scope constant reds six of them). Confirm the replacement coverage by construction before deleting, and cite the case that actually holds the line, not the one that looks adjacent.

Guard tests may grep other files for CODE constructs, but never for PROSE. Task 3554 shipped a ratchet that git-grepped every tracked test module for the literal "skills/" and required each hit to be enumerated in a hand-maintained set; both directions were removed on review. Adding OR removing that substring in a comment/docstring in an unrelated package (escalation/, fused-memory/, orchestrator/, scripts/) red-walled a merge-blocking guard in tests/scripts/ over a diff it does not gate — a cosmetic reword measured "1 failed, 5 passed". It was also a lower bound that missed real consumers containing the token zero times. Do not "fix" this coupling with a word-boundary or regex variant: that preserves the identical dependency on other packages' prose behind a cleverer matcher. Contrast with the legitimate grep-guards in this repo (AST-based ratchets on SpeculativeItem construction sites and on orchestrator.merge_queue.<private> monkeypatch string paths), which assert on code structure, not wording.

CORRECTION to the "sanctioned STRUCTURAL drift guard" carve-out recorded in mem0 b80b78c4 (which cites tests/scripts/test_contributing_lint_command_drift.py and its HTML-comment-marker convention as the approved way to pin a doc against live code). That carve-out is NOT reliably sanctioned and should not be planned as a safe pattern. On task 3465 an architect followed it exactly — bare `<!-- name:begin/end -->` marker spans in skills/escalation-watcher-auto/SKILL.md and OPERATIONS.md, values derived from live producer constants via stdlib `ast` rather than hardcoded, loud-failing extractors that raise instead of returning empty, explicit STRUCTURE-NEVER-WORDING discipline — and reviewer_comprehensive still blocked the whole 769-line module as a documentation/introspection meta-test and mandated deletion. That is the second such data point: task 3544 (mem0 3c294ce3) had a mermaid-vs-TRANSITIONS parity test deleted despite a live in-code oracle. Two independent blocks means the reviewer treats "derived from code at runtime" and "anchored on markers" as insufficient — what it keys on is that the ASSERTION TARGET is doc prose, a module-level/function-body string literal, or a parameter name recovered by introspection. Practical rule for architects: before planning any producer→consumer mirror guard, first check whether the producer's OWN package already asserts those tokens against real produced OUTPUT; on 3465 fused-memory/tests/test_scope_violation_escalator.py already called the real report_rejection() and asserted category/agent_role/severity on the escalation JSON that landed on disk, so the entire guard was redundant with existing behaviour coverage. Same held for its two "premise guard" tests: escalation/tests/test_server.py, escalation/tests/test_queue.py and orchestrator/tests/test_workflow_status_on_resume.py already cover the granted_files grant end-to-end, so an introspection check on the parameter NAME was both redundant and strictly weaker. Also: when deleting such a guard, the doc-side marker spans and any prose sentence claiming the tokens are "pinned by <test file>" must be deleted with it — a SKILL.md is read verbatim as an LLM system prompt, so a dangling reference to a deleted test tells the executing agent a mechanism exists when it does not.

claim: Guard tests should enforce executable code or behavior, not prose, and any replacement coverage must be verified before deleting a guard.

commit_planning's capability-manifest sidecar stamping REWRITES the YAML in canonical block form, and all header comments are LOST. Verified 2026-08-06 on plans/scheduler-dispatch-scoring-and-lock-layer-prd.capability-manifest.yaml: a hand-authored sidecar with a 6-line explanatory header comment came back with zero comment lines, scalars unquoted, long binding strings re-wrapped, and list style normalized — a 393-insertion/318-deletion diff on a 318-line file that was otherwise semantically identical. This is a trap because the committed EXEMPLAR (plans/capability-delivered-checks-prd.capability-manifest.yaml) DOES carry header comments and reads as the house style — but that exemplar was hand-stamped before the stamper existed (its own header says so), so it was never round-tripped through commit_planning. Anyone imitating the exemplar's commented style will silently lose those comments on the first batch flip. Put durable explanation in the .md manifest twin, which is never rewritten; treat the .yaml sidecar as generated-shaped data even though a human authors it first.

ROOT CAUSE (VERIFIED 2026-08-05, still live; block last touched 2026-07-16): plan.json step-SHA provenance gets rewritten so that several distinct steps all record the same "chore: save WIP before inter-iteration rebase" tip. In orchestrator/src/orchestrator/workflow.py::_reconcile_done_step_commits (around lines 8050-8078), for each done step whose recorded commit is no longer an ancestor of HEAD, line 8055 tests whether that step's changed files are a SUBSET of the UNION of files touched by the WIP run, and on a match line 8056 stamps the single wip_tip_sha onto the step. Because it is a subset test over a union, it is DEGENERATE whenever several steps touch the same file(s): every such step matches and all collapse onto the same WIP tip. The precise patch-id remapper git_ops.find_equivalent_commit exists at line 8073 but runs ONLY in the else branch, i.e. only when the coarse heuristic FAILS — the precise mechanism is subordinated to the imprecise one. FIX: reorder to try find_equivalent_commit first; its own comment (8065-8072) already documents it as fully fail-safe (returns None on any git error, unresolvable/GC'd commit, ambiguity, or no equivalent), so promoting it cannot add a failure path. Diagnosed from reify esc-5665-2 (reify task 5665: steps 3/5/7 all recorded 5da1f20c4d; all four commits touched the single file crates/reify-compiler/src/geometry.rs). Filed as dark_factory task 3651. BLAST RADIUS IS LOW: no merge gate or done_provenance consumes plan-step `commit` (done_provenance derives from _merge_sha) and .task/ is gitignored so plan.json never lands in a commit. Real costs are a defeated unbacked-step detector (workflow.py:7303), wasted re-implementation of work already contained in the WIP commit, and escalation noise.

commit_planning manifest-stamper observed behavior (2026-07-22, OS-sandbox batch): the stamper rewrites the YAML sidecar through a YAML round-trip — all hand-written comments are DROPPED and long strings reflowed, so don't put load-bearing information in sidecar comments (put it in the .md manifest twin). It stamps only labels whose tasks are members of the committed batch; sidecar labels belonging to foreign-registry tasks (e.g. reify/sibling flips in a cross-project rollout) are simply left task_id:null WITHOUT appearing in missing_labels (the report tracks batch-tasks-without-sidecar-labels, not the reverse). Foreign-registry labels must be hand-stamped with Edit and the sidecar re-committed (git commit --only) afterwards. Also: commit_planning DOES copy mechanical grep/script delivered_checks into producer metadata.delivered_checks (verified live on task 2910) — the 'interim hand-stamp' note in skills/prd SKILL.md is stale; only foreign-registry ids need hand work.

members.text: Reify agent-harness idiom for waiting on a long cargo build WITHOUT a foreground `sleep` (blocked by the anti-polling guard), a busy-loop (SIGTERMed at the Bash timeout, losing all observations), or a reap-vulnerable background waiter: have the background job write a terminal sentinel to a log, then FOREGROUND-block on `timeout 600 tail -f -n +1 /tmp/<log> | grep -m1 -E "<SENTINEL>" >/dev/null` with the Bash `timeout` set above the `timeout(1)` value. `tail -f | grep -m1` exits ON ITS OWN the moment the sentinel appears, so it is a real blocking wait rather than polling; the `timeout(1)` cap bounds it so the call always returns a NEW TURN (resetting the idle watchdog) even if the build hangs, and you simply re-issue it. Emit the sentinel yourself — e.g. run the job as `{ cargo test ...; echo "EXIT1=$?"; cargo test ...; echo "EXIT3=$?"; } > /tmp/<log> 2>&1` — so one wait covers a whole sequence and the exit codes are in the log. Measured 2026-09-03 (task 5755 architect, cold warm lane `_lane-0`): a targeted `cargo test -p reify-compiler --lib <filter>` + `-p reify-eval --lib geometry_ops` + `-p reify-eval --test <one binary>` sequence finished in ~6 min this way, versus a bare `cargo test -p reify-compiler -p reify-eval` which was abandoned after 8 min still compiling because it must build and link ALL 236 top-level integration binaries under crates/reify-eval/tests/ (`ls crates/reify-eval/tests/*.rs | wc -l`). Always scope to `--lib <filter>` plus `--test <binary>` when confirming specific named tests.

CORRECTION + recipe (measured on task 4152, 2026-08-02, lane _lane-47): a Bash tool command in this harness is hard-killed at ~300s ("Error: command timed out after 300s") regardless of the `timeout` parameter AND regardless of `run_in_background: true`. An existing procedural entry (mem0 d52477fb-acd5-48af-8a7b-48291783be22) claims passing run_in_background:true up front makes the full requested timeout apply — that is FALSE: `cargo test -p reify-eval --lib` was killed at exactly 300s both when auto-backgrounded with timeout=1800000 and when launched with an explicit run_in_background:true. (Could not amend that entry in place: update_memory's content_amend arm is restricted to recon-stage-* agents.)

Working recipe for a long cargo build/test — detach it from the tool's process group with a log + exit sentinel, then poll in sub-300s chunks:
  rm -f /tmp/X.log; setsid nohup bash -c 'command cargo test ... >> /tmp/X.log 2>&1; echo "SENTINEL_EXIT:$?" >> /tmp/X.log' >/dev/null 2>&1 </dev/null &
  for i in $(seq 1 27); do grep -q '^SENTINEL_EXIT:' /tmp/X.log && break; sleep 10; done; grep -E '^SENTINEL_EXIT:|^test result:|^error' /tmp/X.log
Each poll chunk is its own Bash call, so nothing is abandoned when a chunk ends and the turn never ends with work pending. `command cargo` inside the detached bash -c also bypasses the skim PreToolUse condensation wrapper, so the log keeps full per-test output. Reference timings in a warm lane after editing crates/reify-eval/src: `cargo test -p reify-eval --lib` ~9 min wall (262s of test execution, 2263 tests); `cargo clippy -p reify-eval --all-targets -- -D warnings` ~9 min.

Waiting on a backgrounded cargo build from an agent session without sleep-polling (the harness blocks foreground `sleep` loops): find the PID of the background shell with `pgrep -af '<distinctive cargo args>'`, then run in the FOREGROUND `timeout 1500 tail --pid=<PID> -f /dev/null; cat <exit-marker-file>` with a Bash timeout slightly above the inner `timeout`. It blocks on the real process exit and returns cleanly. Measured in a reify warm lane under load ~130: a NEW integration-test file in reify-solver-elastic cold-built in 11 min (its reify-test-support dev-dependency pulls in reify-compiler); rebuilding after editing only form_find.rs took about 1m49s.

When confirming test results in a reify warm lane, capture cargo's OWN exit code — `cargo test ... 2>&1 | tail -N` run in background returns `tail`'s status (always 0), so the harness completion notification reports "exit code 0" even when the test run failed. Use `{ cargo test ... > /tmp/log 2>&1; echo "EXIT=$?"; }` and grep the log for `test result:` lines instead. Separately, a targeted `cargo test -p <crate>` in a lane can take 15+ minutes of wall clock when the merge/verify pipeline's full-workspace `cargo nextest run` is concurrently active, since both contend on the same lane `target/` and CPU — size timeouts accordingly rather than assuming a hang.

claim: For long Cargo runs, write output and the true exit code to a log, then wait in bounded chunks so harness timeouts cannot lose the result.

[SUPERSEDED 2026-09-09 by Leo's ruling] The crate-scoped carve-out recorded below is NOT granted. The house rule is Position A EVERYWHERE: avoid `step-N` plan-step labels in test names, section comments and doc-comments in ALL crates, `crates/reify-syntax/` included. Leo's stated reason, verbatim: "long-term ambiguity is worse than short-term churn." Existing step-N labels in reify-syntax are now CLEANUP DEBT, not sanctioned convention, and a reviewer MAY flag them. The ruling and its deciding evidence live on the canonical record under topic `test-step-n-label-convention`.

HISTORICAL RECORD (recorded 2026-05-16; still factually true, and precisely why cleanup is needed): Convention (crates/reify-syntax/tests/*): test doc-comments may reference task-plan step labels like "step-1", "step-2", "step-3" — this pattern is already established across auto_type_arg_tests.rs and is acceptable shorthand for in-tree readers who can grep adjacent tests for matching step labels. Reviewers should not flag step-N references in isolation when they are consistent with surrounding test labeling.

[VERIFIED 2026-09-09 at HEAD 6c08e5338a] The observation that reify-syntax DID adopt the convention holds: 33 files under `crates/reify-syntax/` carry 187 step-N lines, `tests/harness_syntax/auto_type_arg_tests.rs` among them (14 lines, including `// ── Step-1/2 (task 3665): …` section banners and in-comment cross-references of the form "the step-1 / step-3 tests below"). Only the NORMATIVE force of this entry — "reviewers should not flag" — is withdrawn; the description of what the crate contains is unchanged and remains accurate.
Test doc-comments should use intent-oriented descriptions rather than task-tracking step labels.

In test doc comments, prefer symbolic landmarks (function/branch names, e.g. "the shared Infeasible return after the residual check in solve_core") over hardcoded file:line citations (e.g. "solver.rs:672-682"). Line numbers drift on the next edit and become silently misleading without affecting test behavior. Recent commits applying this convention: `eb80a00afd docs(reify-eval): replace hardcoded line citations with symbolic landmarks` and task 1715's hardcoded GeomRef::Step path replacements.

Test names and comments should describe what is being verified, not reference originating plan-step numbers (avoid `step-1`, `step-N` markers). Plan-step labels are meaningless outside the originating PR and become misleading if the plan is reordered or trimmed.

claim: Test names and comments should describe verified intent using durable symbolic landmarks, not transient plan-step labels or line-number citations.

members.text: Reify dangling-`concurrent.rs`-reference cleanups (task family #6231/#6245/#6276) use TWO distinct fixes, chosen by what the old pointer carried. If content was literally RELOCATED out of the deleted concurrent stack, use the `[Re-homed from `concurrent.rs`'s <symbol>, task ξ #5046 — the dead concurrent stack is deleted by task ο.]` form (examples: engine_edit.rs:6053/6143, engine_fixpoint.rs:1264). If the pointer was merely a "see also / another instance" reader-pointer carrying no relocated content, DELETE it outright — do not convert it to a Re-homed citation, since citing a deleted file for an example nobody can consult is noise. In both cases, live code is referenced by module-qualified SYMBOL name only (e.g. `engine_edit.rs::edit_param`), never by line number.

Reify comment convention, the DELETED-THING half (complements the well-covered "reference symbols, not line numbers" rule — do not restate that one): when a comment must still name a file or symbol that has been DELETED, mark it explicitly as deleted and cite the deleting commit SHA + task, so a reader never tries to open it. Established form, on main at crates/reify-eval/src/engine_edit.rs:6053 and :6143 and crates/reify-eval/src/engine_fixpoint.rs:1264: "[Re-homed from `concurrent.rs`'s <symbol>, task ξ (#5046) — the dead concurrent stack is deleted by task ο.]"; task 6245 reused it as "...was deleted with `concurrent.rs` in c1b8dba3f7 (task ο, #5065)". Decision rule for which way to go: if the surviving sentence stands on its own without the dead thing, DROP the pointer entirely rather than re-homing it; only name the deleted thing when it IS the explanation (why no consumer exists, why a promised guard never arrived). NOTE the SHA-vs-subject-line caveat (mem0 21176f95) does NOT apply here: these cites name commits already LANDED on main, so the SHA is durable — that caveat is about citing unlanded task-branch commits. Ongoing family working this defect class across the workspace: tasks 6218, 6231, 6245, 6253, 6276, 6279, 6316.

DELETED-FILE COROLLARY to the cite-by-symbol convention. When a doc-comment pointer's target is DELETED (not merely drifted), do not scrub the filename — the defect is presenting the file as READABLE, not naming it. House style, established across the reify-eval/reify-runtime concurrent.rs family: name the dead module WITH its deleting commit SHA and owning task, e.g. "deleted with `concurrent.rs` in c1b8dba3f7 (task ο, #5065)" (engine_edit.rs:6082/:6172, engine_fixpoint.rs:1264, task 6231's engine_edit.rs module header, task 6245's gating.rs + commitment.rs). That tells a reader why the consumer is absent and where the history is. So the grep guard for these fixes is "no mention presents the file as readable", NOT "no mention of the file". Two traps seen while working #6245: (1) a removed pointer may be the ONLY statement of what consumes a symbol — check whether the surrounding present-tense claim is now false or orphaned (gating.rs's module header asserted the runtime layer feeds its helpers via NodePolicyOverrides::resolve(), which has had zero production callers since the scheduler died); (2) a forward-looking caveat conditioned on wiring into the deleted subsystem ("NOT wired until task η/3581 lands") is VACUOUS, not pending — retire it in the settled tense rather than preserving it. These fixes are comments-only: a test asserting on the prose, or grepping source for "did the author mention X", is the documentation meta-test anti-pattern — gate on existing suites staying green against a mechanically comments-only diff.

claim: For deleted code references, remove dispensable pointers; retain necessary explanations only with explicit deletion provenance, and never present the deleted target as readable.

members.text: reify harness-layout move mechanics, one more item for the checklist: a test that locates a file from `env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR")` must have that join repointed when it moves into `tests/harness_<sub>/`. `Path::new(env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR")).join("tests/<file>.rs")` becomes `.join("tests/harness_<sub>/<file>.rs")`. This is a RUNTIME panic, not a compile error — the move compiles clean and only the self-reading test reds — so it is invisible to the `#[path]`/`mod` mechanics the other peers cover. Self-reading tests are a real pattern here (`version_id_discipline_gate.rs` set the precedent; `harness_geometry/units_length_closure_guard.rs` cross-checks its own residual cites against its own `// TODO(#NNNN)` comments this way). Also repoint any prose pointer at the old path — e.g. `reify_ir::arg_acceptance`'s module doc names the guard's path. Seen on task #5752.

Rust `#[track_caller]` is INERT when the panic fires inside a closure. A helper written as `x.unwrap_or_else(|| panic!("..."))` reports the closure body's line in helpers.rs, not the calling test's line, because a closure is its own function and does not inherit the attribute from the enclosing fn. Restructure to the `let Some(v) = ... else { panic!("...") };` (let-else) shape so the panic site lives directly in the `#[track_caller]` fn body. Verified empirically with a minimal rustc repro during task #5697; applies to reify-test-support's helpers.rs getters (get_value_cell_in / get_let_expr_in / get_let_expr) and to any assertion helper in that file.

Rust `#[track_caller]` does NOT cross a closure boundary: a panic raised inside `unwrap_or_else(|| panic!(...))` resolves `Location::caller()` to the closure body, silently making the attribute inert so failures report the helper's own line instead of the calling test's. Use the `let Some(x) = ... else { panic!(...) }` shape so the panic site lives directly in the `#[track_caller]` fn body. Verified empirically with a minimal rustc repro during reify task #5697. What #5697 landed in crates/reify-test-support/src/helpers.rs moved the "no template named" panic into a let-else in `get_value_cell_in`, which `get_let_expr_in` reaches it through. It did NOT move the "has no default expr" panic: on main 2b9b48e241 (2026-09-16) that one still sits inside a closure in `require_default_expr`, as does `cell_value`'s panic, and task 6973 is scoped to fix both. Applies to any panicking test-support helper meant to blame its caller. [Corrected 2026-09-16 by the curator sitting per gate task #7578: this entry previously said both `get_value_cell_in` and `get_let_expr_in` were restructured, which overstated the fix.]

To pin that a reify-test-support helper panic reports the CALLER's location (#[track_caller] actually working), add a guard to crates/reify-test-support/tests/track_caller_panic_location.rs (landed by #7612): call its `panic_site(|| ...)` and assert `site.file == file!()` plus a short message substring — never an exact line!() (rustfmt-fragile). The hook there is mutex-serialised and thread-filtered, so it is safe under libtest's parallel threads; don't hand-roll a second panic hook. #[should_panic(expected=..)] pins cannot detect a location regression.

claim: When changing Rust test infrastructure, account for runtime-only behavior and use targeted regression tests to catch failures that compilation cannot reveal.

members.text: Two tests in tests/scripts/ assert on hard wall-clock deadlines and flake under host contention: test_restart_all_orchestrators.py::test_unit_fresh_only_during_grace_still_verifies_and_stamps (VERIFY_TIMEOUT=1 plus a 5s grace window, needing a ~1/sec poll to flip fresh on the 3rd call) and test_spawn_claude.py::test_window_close_yields_129_not_hang (_wait_for_path(pidfile, timeout=5.0) at line 247, polling for a pidfile written by an externally spawned process). Task 3336 saw both fail in one verify run (2 failed / 510 passed in 696.88s) while host load average was 47/87/85 on a 32-core box, then pass 4/4 on isolated re-runs at the identical HEAD. Before treating either as a regression, re-run it in isolation and check `uptime` — a task whose diff does not touch tests/scripts/ is very unlikely to be the cause.

The test_transcript_appearance_suppresses_flag flake (tasks 2344/2361/2365 tracked, host-oversubscription class documented in an earlier memory) has a concrete mechanism: spawn-claude.sh's _started_evidence falls back to _claude_descendant_alive whenever the transcript dir doesn't exist yet at the current poll tick. _claude_descendant_alive shells out to `ps -eo pid=,ppid=,args=` and walks every system process in a pure-bash `while read` loop (O(n) processes, high per-iteration bash overhead) looking for a claude descendant. On a host with ~1165 processes under load average 111-140 on 32 cores, a single call measured ~1.4s in isolation -- enough to consume the entire 3s SPAWN_STARTED_GRACE_SECS grace budget in one _started_watchdog loop iteration, so the loop exits before a second iteration can observe the transcript file that actually appeared almost immediately. Confirmed via bash -x trace + isolated timing on 2026-07-17; reproduces identically on a clean main checkout (not a task-specific regression) and passes cleanly on retry when ambient load allows a call under ~1s. Whoever picks up tasks 2344/2361/2365 should look at bounding/replacing _claude_descendant_alive's full-system ps scan rather than just re-tuning grace/sleep margins.

tests/scripts/test_spawn_claude.py's subprocess-timing tests (test_transcript_appearance_suppresses_flag: grace=3s/sleep=8s; test_foreground_claude_descendant_suppresses_flag_without_transcript: grace=2s/sleep=6s) use generous margins to absorb whole-second `date +%s` truncation noise, but can still spuriously fail under extreme host oversubscription (observed: load avg 116-134 on a 32-core host). Confirmed on task 2286: the full 27-test file failed 1 test on one run, then passed 27/27 clean on immediate retry with no code changes; the failing test also passed standalone in 9.38s. This is the same host-oversubscription flake class already tracked by tasks 2344/2361/2365 — future debugging agents seeing a failure in THIS test file under high load should suspect timing/scheduling flake before assuming a logic regression, and should retry before debugging.

For merge-verify-host-load timing flakes in fixed-second-margin tests, prefer a load-scaled margin over another fixed bump: factor = max(1.0, os.getloadavg()[0] / os.cpu_count()); scaled = ceil(base_secs * factor), clamped to [base_secs, cap_secs]. A fixed bump chases a moving target as host load climbs — tests/scripts/test_spawn_claude.py's SPAWN_STARTED_GRACE_SECS flake recurred within 6 days (task 2367 bumped 1s/2s→3s/8s; task 2733 replaced the fixed values with a `_load_scaled_grace` helper). Floor at base_secs keeps an idle host byte-identical (no regression); cap keeps a pathological host bounded. When enlarging a grace/timeout this way, also make any outer wrapper timeout grace-relative (grace + fixed-work + margin) so the same load spike can't just convert one flake type into another (e.g. a 144 flag-flake into a subprocess TimeoutExpired flake).

Flaky test under merge-worker load: tests/scripts/test_spawn_claude.py::test_transcript_appearance_suppresses_flag can fail with rc 144 ("claude never started within 3s") during full post-merge verify runs on a busy host, because it asserts on real wall-clock timing (3s started-grace vs an 8s fake-claude sleep; watchdog deadline from `date +%s` whole-second resolution). Its docstring already documents the margin as "flaky under load (observed empirically)". It passes reliably in isolation (~9s). When this test is the sole failure in a post-merge verify escalation for a task whose diff does not touch skills/spawn/spawn-claude.sh, treat it as a benign flake and retry the merge rather than modifying task code.

The tests/scripts/ verify suite (declared in tests/scripts/orchestrator.yaml) contains a load-sensitive flake: test_spawn_claude.py::test_normal_spawn_exit0_not_flagged pins SPAWN_STARTED_GRACE_SECS=2 while skills/spawn/spawn-claude.sh:89 defaults it to 90, so under machine load the real spawned subprocess misses the 2s window and the registry records failed-to-start instead of exited. Measured at task 3329: identical trees failed on a 540s run and passed on a 282s run, and the test passes in isolation. Before attributing a red tests/scripts/ run to your own diff, check whether the failure is in a file your diff actually touches and re-run on an idle machine.

claim: Wall-clock-sensitive tests can flake under host load, so check load and rerun failures in isolation before attributing them to a code change.

members.text: The orchestrator's delivered-check dep-gate reads ONLY `metadata.delivered_checks` on the task record. It NEVER reads the `<prd>.capability-manifest.yaml` sidecar. `manifest_stamping.py` copies sidecar checks into task metadata at `commit_planning` and at no other time, so the two surfaces DRIFT and can disagree in three distinct ways: (1) metadata amended post-decompose while the sidecar stays stale (reify task 5758 — its checks were narrowed at esc-5758-4 time, the sidecar still carried the un-narrowed form); (2) metadata carrying checks the sidecar never had (5758 had a 4th D1-pin check absent from the yaml); (3) the task carrying NO `delivered_checks` key at all because it was decomposed before stamping applied to that manifest, making the sidecar's checks entirely INERT (reify task 5261 — verified by direct get_task: no delivered_checks key). Consequence: ANY claim about a check's live gating consequence must be measured against `get_task(<id>).metadata.delivered_checks`, never against the yaml. In a 2026-08-07 audit I made this exact conflation three separate times in one session and reported two false findings before an orchestrator architect caught it. An audit of the sidecars is still valid as an audit OF THE SIDECARS (they are the authoring source of truth, and a future commit_planning re-stamp copies them into live metadata) — it is simply not a measurement of the gate.

orchestrator-reify IS a live systemd `--user` unit — checking it WITHOUT `--user` actively misleads. `systemctl is-active orchestrator-reify.service` returns "inactive"/"could not be found", which led an L2 watcher (2026-07-25/26) to conclude for hours that reify's orchestrator ran as a bare `uv run` process and that journald had no logs for it. Both false. Correct probes: `systemctl --user show orchestrator-reify.service -p MainPID -p ExecMainStartTimestamp -p NRestarts -p Result`, and `journalctl --user -u orchestrator-reify.service`. The root cause of the 2026-07-24..26 fleet-wide dispatch livelock lived in that journal and was unreachable from runs.db, which could record THAT every dispatch requeued but never WHY. Also note `WorkingDirectory=/home/leo/src/dark-factory`, NOT reify's project_root — so any relative path resolved against the orchestrator's cwd resolves into dark-factory.

Operational gotcha: the reify orchestrator runs as a systemd USER unit `orchestrator-reify.service` (managed via `systemctl --user`, alongside sibling user units orchestrator-dark-factory, orchestrator-know-live, etc.). A SYSTEM-scope `systemctl is-active orchestrator-reify.service` FALSELY reports `inactive`/`dead` because the unit lives in the user manager, not the system manager. To check liveness use `systemctl --user is-active orchestrator-reify.service`, or confirm via the escalation MCP port (reify = 127.0.0.1:8100; a listening `orchestrator` process there means it's up), or `ps` for `orchestrator run --config .../reify/orchestrator.yaml`. Corollary: if the escalation MCP tools (resolve_issue, get_pending_escalations, merge_request) respond successfully, the orchestrator is up by definition — don't separately conclude it's down from a system-scope systemctl check.

CORRECTION — THE REIFY ORCHESTRATOR *IS* A SYSTEMD USER UNIT (verified live 2026-08-29). A prior belief that it was "not under systemd, check the process/port 8100 instead" is FALSE and cost at least one investigation real accuracy. `systemctl --user status orchestrator-reify.service` returns Active: active (running), Main PID a `uv` process, CGroup under user@1000.service/app.slice; the unit file is ~/.config/systemd/user/orchestrator-reify.service (enabled) with a drop-in at orchestrator-reify.service.d/warm-lane.conf. TWO CONSEQUENCES: (1) its LOGS ARE ON DISK in the user journal — `journalctl --user -u orchestrator-reify.service` works. An earlier pass believed its stdout was an unrecoverable socket and reasoned from correlation instead of reading the log; it is journald's socket. (2) The namespace is `systemctl --user`, NOT system scope — a system-scope probe returns nothing and looks exactly like proof that no unit exists, which is very likely how the false claim was minted. Restart discipline is unchanged: never `systemctl restart` it directly (the TimeoutStopSec=90 stop window cancels restart's start half); use scripts/orchestrator-redeploy-restart.sh.

claim: Verify operational behavior against the correct live source and namespace; stale sidecars and wrong-scope systemd checks can both produce false conclusions.

members.text: Gotcha when adding a new `await self.git_ops.<method>(...)` call inside TaskWorkflow._execute_iterations or _verify_debugfix_loop: the established loop-driver test harnesses (test_workflow_resume_on_progress.py `_stub_iteration_helpers`, test_workflow_zero_output_hang.py) wire git_ops as a plain MagicMock, so awaiting a new git_ops method raises `TypeError: object MagicMock can't be used in 'await' expression`. Make the new call fail-soft (try/except, default a safe value) if it is observability-only, or update those harnesses to AsyncMock the method. These harnesses already stub `_get_head_commit` as AsyncMock(return_value='abc123') and mock `append_iteration_log`, so adding extra `_get_head_commit()` calls is safe and they do not assert iteration-entry contents.

In fused-memory tests, a sync MagicMock's assert_not_called() will fail the repo-wide style check (tests/test_check_asyncmock_assertion_style.py, task 525) if any assert_not_awaited() appears in the SAME test function — the checker flags the mix without knowing one of the mocks is sync. Fix by asserting mock.call_count == 0 for the sync mock instead of converting it to an async-style helper.

Gotcha (orchestrator tests): when a workflow method on the VERIFY/REVIEW loop path gains a new `await self.git_ops.<method>(...)` call (e.g. task 2760's `_commit_amendment_wip` awaiting `git_ops.has_uncommitted_work`), every loop-driving test helper that builds `git_ops` as a bare `MagicMock` breaks with `TypeError: object MagicMock can't be used in 'await' expression`. The bare MagicMock returns a non-awaitable child. members.text: In this environment, multi-line heredoc commit messages via `git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF' ... EOF)"` in the Bash tool can get mangled (newlines collapsed, command corrupted with a stray "skim" token inserted) — root cause not diagnosed. Workaround: write the commit message to a temp file with the Write tool and commit via `git commit -F <tmpfile>` instead.

Git commit gotcha in this harness's Bash tool: backticks inside a double-quoted `git commit -m "..."` are shell command substitution and SILENTLY DELETE the quoted word. Writing -m "...mistaken for `limit` positionally..." runs `limit` as a command, emits "limit: command not found" to stderr, and stores the message with an empty gap where the identifier was — while git still reports success, so the corruption is easy to miss. This matters here because dark-factory commit messages routinely quote code identifiers in backticks. The existing "use multiple -m flags instead of a heredoc" entry (id cc001d17) does NOT fix this — backticks are substituted in any double-quoted -m string regardless of how many -m flags are used. Reliable fix: write the message to a file with a QUOTED heredoc delimiter (cat > /tmp/msg.txt <<'MSGEOF' ... MSGEOF) and commit with `git commit -F /tmp/msg.txt`; the quoted delimiter disables all interpolation. Same fix repairs an already-corrupted message via `git commit --amend -F`. Verify with `git log -1 --format=%B | grep` for the identifier rather than trusting the exit code.

Writing a git commit message via `git commit -m` with a double-quoted string in Bash shell-substitutes any backtick-quoted code span, silently deleting it from the committed message (observed on task 3341: a message containing a backtick-quoted "is True" committed as "strict :" and emitted "is: command not found"). Use a quoted heredoc to a temp file plus `git commit -F <file>`, or keep backticks out of -m messages entirely.

Git gotcha (2026-07-06): to commit ONLY specific UNTRACKED files while leaving unrelated modified/staged files out (e.g. a PRD + manifest committed to main amid other sessions' live WIP), `git commit -F msg -- <path1> <path2>` FAILS on untracked paths with 'error: pathspec ... did not match any file(s) known to git' — git commit with a pathspec only sees tracked/staged paths. Correct sequence: `git add -- <paths>` FIRST, THEN `git commit -F msg -- <paths>` — the explicit pathspec still commits ONLY those paths (the --only default when paths are given), so other concurrently-staged content stays out of your commit. This composes with the existing df convention: run it as `setsid git commit ... &` + poll the log, because pre-commit runs the full 3× pyright (fused-memory/orchestrator/dashboard) and exceeds the 2-min Bash ceiling even for a docs-only commit.

`git commit -F <file>` accepts ANY readable path, inside or outside the repo working tree. The only constraint is ARGUMENT ORDER: `-F <path>` must appear BEFORE any `--` pathspec separator. After `--`, git parses the value as a pathspec, and a pathspec outside the repo yields `fatal: <path>: '<path>' is outside repository at '<repo>'` — which is the error that has repeatedly been misattributed to the file's LOCATION.

Empirically established 2026-07-31 (git 2.43.0, throwaway repo, message file at an out-of-repo /tmp path):
  A) `git commit -F /tmp/msg.txt`                → SUCCEEDS, rc=0, message applied verbatim
  B) `git commit -F /tmp/msg.txt -- f.txt`       → SUCCEEDS (-F before the separator)
  C) `git commit -- f.txt -F /tmp/msg.txt`       → FAILS with the "outside repository" fatal

Consequence: the widely-repeated prescription to copy the message file INTO the repo tree first (e.g. `<repo>/.commit-msg.txt`) is unnecessary cargo-cult. It "works" only because it incidentally makes the misparsed pathspec fall inside the repo, masking the ordering bug rather than fixing it. This resolved escalation esc-3249-1, which had three mutually-contradictory Mem0 entries on the subject; the resolution was that BOTH sides described real observations and the true variable was ordering, not path location.

Multi-line git commit messages: use `git commit -F -` with a heredoc, NOT `git commit -m "$(cat <<'MSG' ... MSG)"`. The Bash tool's eval wrapper collapses newlines between statements before the shell sees them, so the command-substitution form arrives as one line and dies with `syntax error near unexpected token '('` (exit 127) — the whole commit is lost, not degraded. The `-F -` heredoc form survives the same wrapper intact and was used for every commit on task 3199. Same root cause as the reify `pkill-pgrep-self-match` eval-wrapper note; this is its git-commit instance. Related: prefer one logical command per Bash call, and write `tail -n N` not `tail -N`.

claim: For reliable Git commits, write complex messages to a file and pass it with `git commit -F` before any `--` pathspecs; stage untracked paths before committing them.

members.text: In orchestrator/tests/, a deferred `from dashboard.data.orchestrator import read_task_artifacts` (or any cross-subproject import not among orchestrator/shared/escalation) raises ModuleNotFoundError/reportMissingImports even though the root conftest.py wires all workspace subprojects' src/ onto sys.path. Cause: verify.py runs `uv run --project orchestrator pytest orchestrator/tests/...`, which makes pytest resolve rootdir/confcutdir to orchestrator/ (via orchestrator/pyproject.toml's [tool.pytest.ini_options]) — pytest never ascends above confcutdir to load the repo-root conftest.py, and orchestrator/tests/conftest.py only sys.path-inserts orchestrator/shared/escalation src dirs, not dashboard's. Fix pattern (used in test_lane_lifecycle_integration.py, task 2260): add a module-local sys.path.insert for the needed subproject's src/ directly in the test file (mirroring conftest.py's own idiom but scoped to that file), plus a `# pyright: ignore[reportMissingImports]` comment on the import line (pyright doesn't execute runtime sys.path mutations, and orchestrator/pyproject.toml's [tool.pyright] extraPaths also omits dashboard/src). This same `# pyright: ignore[reportMissingImports]` convention for cross-subproject deferred test imports is already established in dashboard/tests/test_costs_data.py and escalation/tests/test_*.py.

In scripts/legibility/, a bare sibling `import config` (e.g. in census.py) resolves correctly at real runtime (pytest via conftest.py's sys.path insert, and `python scripts/legibility/census.py` via Python's own script-dir-as-sys.path[0]) but is a FALSE POSITIVE under `pyright scripts/legibility/<file>.py` run from the repo root: pyright picks up the unrelated top-level `<repo-root>/config/` directory (an implicit PEP 420 namespace package holding usage-accounts.yaml) instead of scripts/legibility/config.py, producing a spurious "X is not a known attribute of module config" error. Harmless — the root pyproject.toml's `[tool.pyright] include = ["conftest.py"]` doesn't cover scripts/ at all, so this never gates a real merge; verify actual behavior via `python scripts/legibility/<file>.py` directly rather than trusting a standalone pyright run.

In dark-factory, fused-memory tests that dynamically import a sibling script via `sys.path.insert(scripts_dir); import <script_name>` (e.g. test_cgl_eta_finalize_gate.py, test_clear_false_dependency_invalidations.py) can fail pyright with reportMissingImports even though fused-memory/pyproject.toml's extraPaths already lists "scripts"/"tests". Cause: the verify harness's scoped/targeted type-check command runs `uv run --project fused-memory pyright fused-memory/<path>...` from the repo root WITHOUT `--directory fused-memory`, so pyright loads the root-level pyproject.toml's fallback [tool.pyright] config instead (extraPaths there only has each subproject's src/, not fused-memory/scripts or fused-memory/tests). This is pre-existing/systemic, not specific to any one task — reproduced identically against the already-merged test_clear_false_dependency_invalidations.py. Fix within task scope: add `# pyright: ignore[reportMissingImports]` on the `import <script_name>` line (established codebase convention, see orchestrator/tests/test_session_hooks.py, shared/tests/test_task_statuses.py) rather than editing root/shared pyproject.toml (out of scope, wrong layer, large blast radius).

scripts/tests/ (e.g. scripts/legibility/*.py) is verified via `uv run --project shared pytest scripts/tests/...` — this scopes execution to shared/pyproject.toml's own dependency set (pydantic, pydantic-settings, aiosqlite, pyyaml, python-dotenv only). Packages like jsonschema, ruamel.yaml, etc. that are only transitive deps of other workspace members (fused-memory, orchestrator, escalation per their uv.lock) are NOT importable there, even though they may appear available in an ambient/full-workspace venv. When writing a scripts/ module, verify package availability against `uv run --project shared python -c "import X"`, not the interactive dev shell's venv. This convention is load-bearing: see `_FALLBACK_UV_PROJECT = 'shared'` in orchestrator/src/orchestrator/verify.py and the comment in shared/pyproject.toml (task 2070).

claim: Repository tooling is project-scoped, so validate imports and type checks in the exact execution context rather than assuming workspace-wide paths, dependencies, or configuration.

In reify, any trait-conformance walk (`reify_eval::conforms_to_trait` / `conforms_to_output`) MUST be resolved against MERGED module + prelude trait defs: a user module's `CompiledModule.trait_defs` holds only the traits that module itself declares, so `structure def X : Rigid` compiles to an EMPTY `trait_defs` and the `Rigid : Physical` refinement edge (stdlib/structural_physical.ri) exists only in the prelude. Passing the bare module set type-checks and silently degrades the walk to direct-bound matching with no diagnostic. gui/src-tauri/src/engine.rs now encodes this as a `MergedTraitDefs` newtype (private field, only `merged_trait_defs(module, prelude)` fills it, `empty()` is `#[cfg(test)]`), so the degraded call is a compile error rather than a silent behaviour change.

[CORRECTED 2026-09-16 by memory_consolidator, run d4e55cc3]: The preceding "gui/src-tauri/src/engine.rs now encodes this..." sentence describes task #5558's OWN BRANCH state only, as observed 2026-09-15 by that task's implementer. Re-verified 2026-09-16 via get_task(5558): status is still `in-progress`, with a `merge_retry_pending` entry (branch_head fa92746e, base_sha 43a442d8) showing the branch has NOT yet merged to main. Do not treat the MergedTraitDefs fix as shipped in mainline until task 5558 actually merges. This mirrors the identical premature-completion framing already corrected on sibling peer 62e91e92 (same topic `reify-traitdefs-prelude-merge-required`), which states main still uses the literal `.contains("Physical")` substring check.

In reify-eval, `Engine::default_kernel_name.is_none()` is an exact test for exactly one thing: "this ENGINE INSTANCE holds no geometry kernel". `default_kernel_name` is a field on the Engine INSTANCE (`crates/reify-eval/src/lib.rs:455`), not a property of the linked binary.

Constructor mechanism (unchanged and still correct): `Engine::with_prelude` sets `default_kernel_name = geometry_kernel.map(...)`, so a `None` kernel yields `None` (`crates/reify-eval/src/engine_admin.rs:231-236`); `with_registered_kernel{,s}` derive it from `pick_lexmin_brep_kernel`, whose helper `pick_lexmin_brep_kernel_in` (`crates/reify-eval/src/kernel_registry.rs:211-219`) ends in `.or_else(|| registered.values().next())` and therefore returns `None` if and only if the static inventory registry is empty.

CORRECTED 2026-09-08 (curator sitting; verified against reify main @ efbc0932bd). This entry previously framed the predicate as an EXACT test for "this BINARY registered no geometry kernel at all (i.e. stub mode)". That binary-level reading is FALSIFIED, and it fails in BOTH directions:
- It can never be TRUE on a shipped binary. `crates/reify-kernel-manifold/src/register.rs:62-69` emits its `KernelRegistration` via `inventory::submit!` with NO `#[cfg]` gate, and `crates/reify-cli/src/main.rs:20`'s `extern crate reify_kernel_manifold as _;` is likewise unconditional, so the "manifold" key is always present in a shipped CLI's registry, the empty-inventory branch is unreachable, and even a stub (no-OCCT) build gets `Some("manifold")` — a Mesh-only kernel. (Refinement first recorded 2026-08-26 from mem0 9d0b91b6-aed7-4b3e-a63c-9e2c3a60b7f3; now promoted from caveat to correction.)
- It is routinely TRUE on a fully kernel-equipped binary. `Engine::new(checker, None)` is PRODUCTION CLI code (`crates/reify-cli/src/main.rs:947, 1100, 1983, 2127, 2287`) and is the shape behind the test helper `make_simple_engine` (`crates/reify-test-support/src/helpers.rs:106-108`). Those instances have an empty kernel map and `default_kernel_name == None` on a fully OCCT-equipped build.

Read it therefore ONLY as an instance guard — which is what its legitimate call sites do, e.g. `measure_dfm_rules`'s "C1 guard: no default kernel → nothing to measure" (`crates/reify-eval/src/engine_constraints.rs:1603-1606`), correct precisely because it asks about the instance. To ask instead "can this build produce or tessellate a BRep", the honest predicate is CAPABILITY, not presence: `Engine::has_repr_capable_kernel()` (`crates/reify-eval/src/engine_constraints.rs:894`; the discriminator `unmeasured_reason` uses at :812), i.e. `CapabilityDescriptor::supports_any_repr(ReprKind::BRep)` read off the `KernelRegistration`. Conflating the two produces user-facing diagnostics that falsely tell an OCCT-enabled user to rebuild with OCCT.

The normative form of this rule, and the instance-vs-linked-binary distinction spelled out, live in the preferences_and_norms peer under topic `reify-engine-default-kernel-name-predicate`.

Reify, capability direction of the synthetic-kernel-key gotcha (task 6169, cost two review cycles): you cannot answer "does THIS engine hold a BRep-capable kernel?" by looking the engine's own `geometry_kernels` names up in the static inventory registry. Because `Engine::with_registered_kernel` (the constructor every production constraint-dispatching surface uses — reify-cli main.rs:604/999/1564, gui EngineSession) files its pick under the synthetic `Engine::DEFAULT_KERNEL_NAME`, that lookup MISSES on every shipped binary and silently degrades to whatever the unregistered-kernel default is (a benefit-of-the-doubt `true` in 6169's case), making any arm gated on the answer dead code on exactly the surfaces it was written for. The fix shape that works: record the answer at CONSTRUCTION, where the `KernelRegistration` is still in hand (`(reg.descriptor)().supports_any_repr(ReprKind::BRep)` stored into an `Option<bool>` field), and keep the registry scan only as a fallback for `Engine::new(_, Some(stub))` test seams. Note the divergence is invisible on an OCCT build — both answers coincide — so the gate that makes it observable everywhere is a structural pin asserting the engine's own kernel names are ABSENT from the registry, not a behavioural test.

[CORRECTED 2026-08-26]: A prior append to this entry claimed "CONFIRMED 2026-08-26: task 6169 landed this fix as `Engine::repr_capable_kernel: Option<bool>` (recorded at construction time from the `KernelRegistration`)." That claim was FALSE, verified this stage: a repo-wide case-insensitive grep for `repr_capable_kernel` across the reify repo returns zero matches (the field does not exist in the codebase), and task 6169's live status is `pending`, not `done` — no fix has landed. Treat this gotcha as UNRESOLVED. Do not re-assert completion until task 6169 reaches status=done AND the field is confirmed present in the codebase via grep. This entry previously absorbed a same-day near-duplicate note (mem0 3ae219c3, deleted, consolidated here) that restated the same gotcha with less detail.

[RESOLVED 2026-09-09]: Both conditions the 2026-08-26 correction set are now MET, each re-verified first-hand this sitting rather than taken from another record. (1) Task 6169's live status is `done`, with `done_provenance.kind = merged`. (2) The field EXISTS: `Engine::repr_capable_kernel: Option<bool>` is declared in crates/reify-eval/src/lib.rs, and the wiring matches the fix shape prescribed above exactly. It is initialised to `None` in the plain constructor in `engine_admin.rs` — whose own comment says the caller-supplied-kernel seam "leaves it None and gets the benefit-of-the-doubt scan" — and overwritten with `Some(..)` by BOTH inventory-driven constructors in that same file: the single-pick path stores `picked.is_some_and(|reg| (reg.descriptor)().supports_any_repr(ReprKind::BRep))` right after `with_prelude`, and the multi-kernel path stores the `any(..)` of the same descriptor predicate across the registry. It is consumed by `Engine::has_repr_capable_kernel` in `engine_constraints.rs`, which returns the construction-recorded answer when present and falls back to the registry scan only when it is `None`; `engine_build.rs` destructures the field explicitly so a later field addition cannot silently skip it, and the structural pin lives in crates/reify-eval/tests/representation_within_assertion.rs. The gotcha in the body above is therefore RESOLVED on main — keep it as the design precedent for the synthetic-key class (record the answer where the registration is still in hand), not as a live defect. Cite by SYMBOL (`Engine::repr_capable_kernel`, `Engine::has_repr_capable_kernel`), never by line number: this entry's own `main.rs:604/999/1564` anchors are the kind that rot.

claim: In Reify, evaluate traits and kernel capabilities from authoritative, context-appropriate data rather than incomplete module or registry clues.

That is fine for a test that only greps the copy's source text, but any test that actually EXECUTES it (e.g. --print-plan) must materialize $dir/scripts/ with the whole sibling set plus $dir/.config/nextest.toml. Do NOT hand-roll the file list and do NOT trim it to verify.sh's seven DIRECT `source` lines — several entries are transitive under an already-copied lib. In reify, tests/infra/test_verify_throughput.sh and test_verify_gui_feature_check.sh auto-discover every `source "$SCRIPT_DIR/..."` lib line in their fixture copy of scripts/verify.sh and HARD-FAIL if that lib was not copied into the throwaway repo. So adding a new sourced *-lib.sh to verify.sh forces updating those fixtures' copy lists. Reading a non-sourced .txt config inline (guarded by `[ -f ]`, degrading to empty when absent) avoids this entirely and is the preferred pattern for new verify.sh config data.

Reify verify gotcha — adding a NEW integration test to a "consolidatable" crate (the 5 listed in tests/infra/harness-layout-lib.sh, e.g. reify-eval) as a top-level `crates/<c>/tests/<file>.rs` FAILS the verify preflight `./scripts/check-harness-baseline-registration.sh --from-git` with `HARNESS_BASELINE_REG FAIL ... reason=unregistered-standalone`. This is a PREFLIGHT: it aborts verify before the test/lint/type steps ever run, so all three verify logs show only this one error and the crate's real test/clippy status is unknown (re-run them yourself after fixing).

Remedy (do NOT grandfather): move the file to `crates/<c>/tests/harness_<subsystem>/<file>.rs` and declare it from the `harness_<subsystem>.rs` root with an EXPLICIT `#[path = "harness_<subsystem>/<file>.rs"] mod <file>;`. The `#[path]` is mandatory and separately enforced (C1 mandate): a bare `mod <file>;` in an integration-test crate root resolves to the sibling top-level `tests/<file>.rs`, not the subdir. Keeping the module stem-named preserves every test's `<file>::<test>` module path, so existing `test(/^<file>::/)`-shaped filtersets keep resolving; only the binary id changes (BT-2 scans for repo-resident selectors naming a consolidated stem).

Adding a row to tests/infra/harness-layout-baseline.manifest is SUPERSEDED (Leo, 2026-07-22, esc-5056-11) — the manifest is a shrinking ratchet, not an allow-list to grow.

Shared harness includes (`#[path = "common/differential.rs"] mod differential;`) belong at the harness ROOT, not inside the consuming submodule (matches harness_selective_demand.rs); submodules then reach it via `use crate::differential::{...};`. rustc compiles one copy per binary either way, so root placement stops a second consumer silently duplicating the include.

Verify the fix with `./scripts/check-harness-baseline-registration.sh --from-git` (expect `violations=0`) plus `bash tests/infra/test_harness_kloc_cap.sh`, which live-scans every harness root for the `#[path]` mandate and the stale-selector (BT-2) condition.

members.text: When adding a second ref arm to hooks/reference-transaction, do NOT copy the refs/heads/main arm's zero-OLD housekeeping filter (`[ -z "${_old//0/}" ] && continue`, hooks/reference-transaction:79). Measured on git 2.43.0: `git stash push` presents old=0000000000... on refs/stash even when the stack is already NON-empty (a 2nd push onto a 1-entry stack logged old=0000000 new=c213482). Copying that filter into a refs/stash arm makes the guard silently never fire while still logging as installed — a dead instrument that reads as protection. The zero-OLD filter is correct ONLY for refs/heads/main, where an all-zero old genuinely means pack-refs/gc ref creation.

git's reference-transaction hook can only guard the PUSH direction of refs/stash, never pop/drop. Measured on git 2.43.0 in throwaway repos (task 5981): `git stash push` fires the hook on ref=refs/stash in both "prepared" and "committed", and exiting non-zero in "prepared" aborts it with rc 128 while PRESERVING the working tree and leaving the stash stack unchanged. But `git stash pop` and `git stash drop` of a NON-LAST entry fire NO reference-transaction hook at all (git rewrites the stash reflog instead of the ref); only a last-entry drop, a last-entry pop's trailing drop, and `git stash clear` reach a ref DELETION transaction — and in the pop case the working-tree apply PRECEDES the deletion, so refusing it cannot prevent WIP injection. `git stash create` and `git stash apply <ref>` never touch refs/stash at all, so a private-ref park path (dark-factory's refs/dark-factory/merge-park) keeps working with such a guard armed.

RECOVERY STEP for the warm-lane `git stash` hazard (complements the existing "NEVER use git stash in a warm lane" entry, mem 5fc4ca73-cc2c-4988-9fc5-385ca2092c13, which covers the pop-a-foreign-stash mechanism and the rr-cache risk but NOT this aftermath). After a bad `git stash pop` conflict in a lane, git leaves BOTH `MERGE_RR` and a zero-byte `MERGE_RR.lock` in the per-worktree git dir at /home/leo/src/reify/.git/worktrees/<lane>/. These persist after you resolve the conflict and after `git checkout HEAD -- <file>`, and they poison every SUBSEQUENT `git commit` in that lane: observed 2026-07-30 in _lane-22 as one `git commit` dying with "Segmentation fault (core dumped)" and the next failing with "fatal: Unable to create '.../worktrees/<lane>/MERGE_RR.lock': File exists" and exit 128. In both cases the commit object was still CREATED and the branch ref DID move — so check `git log --oneline -1` before assuming the commit failed and retrying (a blind retry would double-commit). Fix: confirm no operation is in progress (none of MERGE_HEAD, MERGE_MSG, CHERRY_PICK_HEAD, REVERT_HEAD, rebase-merge, rebase-apply exist in that dir), then `rm -f <dir>/MERGE_RR.lock <dir>/MERGE_RR`. Both are regenerated by git on the next real conflict, so removing them when no merge is in flight is safe. Also check whether an rr-cache preimage was written under /home/leo/src/reify/.git/rr-cache/<hash>/ (rerere.enabled is true repo-wide); if the write failed with "No such file or directory" nothing was recorded and there is nothing to clean.

claim: Treat git stash as unsafe in warm lanes: hooks cannot block every stash operation, and conflict aftermath can poison later commits, so avoid stash and verify commits before retrying.

1. `git diff --name-only $(git merge-base HEAD main)..HEAD` — is the failing artifact even in your diff?
2. `git log --oneline $(git merge-base HEAD main)..main -- <failing-file>` — the killer. It lists exactly the main-side commits your base is missing FOR THAT FILE. members.text: gmsh 4.15.2 deadlocks inside gmshModelMeshGenerate(3) when a PostView background mesh-size field is evaluated from many mesher threads. The threshold is fixture-dependent, so a single measurement does not generalise: on a clean process meshing a unit cube, General.NumThreads=8 completes in ~4s while 32 hangs indefinitely; in tests/mesher_poison_recovery.rs, whose gmsh has already been through a finalize/initialize recovery cycle, 8 already hangs. It is a true block, not slowness (CPU time frozen, all threads in futex_do_wait), and Mesh.MaxNumThreads3D=1 does not avoid it. reify's fix (task #7447) pins General.NumThreads=1 unconditionally in refine_volume_with_size_field. Consequence for test authors: a regression guard for this must ask for a thread count measured to hang ON ITS OWN FIXTURE — copying a count that hangs a different binary silently yields a test that is green on both sides of the fix.

ROOT CAUSE of the gmsh 4.15.2 PostView background-field deadlock (task #7706, supersedes the 'finalize/initialize cycle' hypothesis): gmsh 4.15.2's PViewData::searchScalar/Vector/Tensor (src/post/PViewData.cpp ~L323-415) build the view's OctreePost LAZILY behind an orphaned `#pragma omp barrier` + `#pragma omp single`. 1D/2D meshing run `#pragma omp parallel for schedule(dynamic)` over curves/surfaces (Generator.cpp ~L431/L590), so when General.NumThreads exceeds the number of classified curves, idle threads sit at the loop-end barrier while working threads hit the octree barrier -> futex deadlock. Measured with a Python repro of refine_volume_with_size_field's FFI sequence: unit cube (14 curves after classify_surfaces PI/12) passes at 14 threads and hangs at 15; open triangle (3 curves) passes at 3 and hangs at 4. That is the whole 'fixture-dependent threshold'. FIX (measured 0 hangs in 48 runs at 2..32 threads, both fixtures): call gmshViewProbe once on the calling thread after view_add_list_data and before mesh_generate. Outside a parallel region the orphaned barrier/single bind to a team of one, so the octree gets built single-threaded; `_octree` is only deleted in the PViewData destructor. Upstream master (gmsh-git snapshot 2026-09-29, versioned 5.0.0) replaced it with `_getOctree()` under `#pragma omp critical(PViewDataOctree)`. No release past 4.15.2 existed on PyPI or conda-forge on 2026-10-01.

reify PLAN-FILES HYGIENE peer (topic harness-layout-gate-decision-rule; the gate/remedy rule itself is canonical bbc063a7 + peer dbada1e1 — this adds only the plan-time failure mode).
